It is not so much the I break out as a new Society game. case in Scotland, but in England . a married women's maiden name is seldom mentioned, and it is often the case that it is quite unknown to her dearest friends. In trance and Belgium, on the contrary, it is not uncommon for constant use to be made of the earlier dignity, and a woman is cited in a court Of law by hr maiden name in addition to that of her histband. This is also the case in Scotland where, generally speaking, i women have greater equality of rights than obtains n England. But many protests are being made, and many declare they will follow the example of Miss Brown. who says that when she marries Mr. Rohl son, she will havo her visiting cards engraved Mrs. Robinson-Brown. Our Colonial Sisters.—Mrs. Humphrey Ward, who is a native of Hobart, the capital of Tasruaaia, nlturallv speaks enthusiastically of Colonial women and says that it will be to the Colonies that we shall have to look for the highest type of womanl-ood. It has always been -our habit to look upon our Colonial sisters as hard- working' domesticated women, bat not very ctiltured,or polished in their manners and appearance. But things -.have advanced very far in Canada and Australia during the past forty or fifty years. In education, in mental and moral development they have higher ideals than we .aav ,and life in the colonies is not narrowed, and so axclusive as it is rendered in this country by social con- ventions. Moreover they have in a much larger measure a direct voice in the making of the conditions under which hey live. It is her greater knowledge and experienee of matters of the outer world, her practical domestic training, and her testa for the higher cultures, that induces Mrs. Humphrey Ward to think that, before long -the Colonies will lead the way in producing the highest type of womanhood. Vegetarianism Fashionable.—Among the smart folk, vegetarianism is greatly on the increase. Fruit takes the foremost place, and rice, cheese, toast, macaroni and nuts, form the most -important dishes. Foreign fruits are in greatsrlemand by fashionable vegetarians, and on their -tables per- simmons, custard apples, guavas front Marierin, and grape fruit from Jamaica, may generally be found. Teen the recent South African Exhibition has brought several new fruits, and preserves, to our notice, end the majority of fruit eaters find small pine apples, fig jelly, wickson plums, and the Cape gooseberry, particularly toothsome. Qeite a new dish among vegetarians is liquid cheese served boiling, and eaten with toasr,while the latest salad is made of two-fifths apple, to three- fifths celery, a compound that tastes better than one might suppose from the description. Evening Hairdressing and Ornamentations at the Theatres.—When we take into consideration all that has been and still is said and written about the matinee hat —and with good cause—we cannot but marvel that the modish fashion of dressing and ornamenting the hair in -the evening should be so lightly passed by and tolerated by theatre goers. It is a fact that two fashionably dressed heads blot out, the stage as effectively as the same number of matinee hats, Net comparatively little is said about the practice which is at once ridiculous and wholly selfish. WEDNES WONTE'N DELITNEC IN NV ITIRTNGTON

I At the Warrington Police Court on Nlonday„ three ! respectal)ly-dressed Widnes womon named Sarah Kone, ; Esther Gordon. and Sarah Maguire, pleaded guilty to I having been drunk and incapable in Bridge-street at 5.15 on Saturday night.—lnspector Taylor stated that he saw the prisoners come off the Central Station at : 8.5. They were staggering drunk, and were followed ; along. the street by a largo crowd. They walked into Walker's Vaults, and were immediately ejected. Then j prisoners were followed by a still bigger crowd along liorsernarket-street, and the street was that full of !people that it was di,licult to make a way through. In Bridge-street prisoners went into another hotel, and Iwere put out. The crowd still kept growing, and prisoners in the centre looked like little children. Witness put them in a cab, and conveyed them to the I Police Station. They were not supplied with any drink in Warrington. Superintendent Monaghan said prisoners were drunk when they arrived from Widnes. They came to Warrington to see some friends. On Snnday they were bailed ont.—Prisoners were each fined lis, including costs.

div.head: STORY FROM WARRINGTON.
div.p: A STORY FROM WARRINGTON.
The Exaraihei, Satuiday, June 8, 1907
WOMAN'S REALM.
been hired from. For this purpose he had been disguised as a groom who was hiring the "turn out" for the evening for his master. The next clay he was in Brighton.

The hue a-nd cry over the-disappearance of Golightly T. Hankey was immense. The beach at Dover was scoured, docks dragged, everything done to discover the missing man, but to no effect. A prisoner under fathoms of water he was securely hidden.
He refused to pay any ransom. The days passed into a week, and still he was obdurate. Sooner than pay a ransom they might keep him for ever.

Meanwhile, the Greaser haunted Brighton and . its environs. He was .walking down the parade when his arm was touched. He turned and found that the hand that touched him belonged to the girl he had hoped never to see again. It was Mamie Chessleridge ! " Involuntarily a cry escaped him. "Mamie You here?"

"Yes, Mr. Rising," addressing him by the name he had given her in Yorkshire. "I am in great trouble. I want your help." If I can, Mamie," he said, wonderingly. "Find Poppa," she said, briefly. ".Your father Is he lost? Why, he can- not be the millionaire Hankey? "
"He is, Ted," she said, ailing back to the old Harrogate days. "I call him Poppa, be- cause he has brought me up from childhood. And oh! it is killing me. I am afraid he must be dead."

The Greaser was astounded. This was the strangest trick Fate had ever played him. To have kidnapped the guardian Of the girl beloved! "Come out of this crush, Mamie, where we can talk freely and quietly." He offered her his arm, and she took ie. naturally. The Greaser was undone completely. Here was the girl he had put behind him, after a tre- mendous struggle, still a factor in his life. "Can you find him, °Ted? Can you find him?"

He looked at her face; it was pale and drawn with sorrow and anxiety, and he made an oath to himself that the obstinate old millionaire should pay up at once for the sake of his ward and the love she had for him.

" Mamie," he said, "I told you in Harro- gate I was not a good man. I am not. I made that confession to you because I love you. It is because I am what I am that I may be able to aid you. Promise me secrecy upon your part and I will do my best to discover him for you."
i Needless to add the pledge was given readily enough, and the smiles came back to 1 the face of Mamie.
Wiring in code to the rendezvous for them to meet him—the Greaser—that night, he joined the Submarine in the backwaters of the Crouch.

The One-eyed Man and Bresci had almost despaired of, making the millionaire amen- able; indeed, the One-eyed Man said to the Greaser, as he joined them in the private cabin: "Greaser, he's a tough nut; he'll not part with a cent. Says he'll bally well rot first!"

"I'm here to make him," said the Greaser. " Shew me to him." He was led into the cabin occupied by the millionaire, who, when he saw his visitor, broke into a fury, for he recognised riim as "Howard T. Egerton ". "You—you skunk! Not a cent if I rot on your craft," he cried. "You'll pay up to-night, sir," said the Greaser. "Failing that, Mamie Chessleridge joins you to-morrow." It was an empty threat, for the Greaser would never have allowed a hair of her head to be touched., But it conquered Hankey; : love for his ward won where force had failed.

"You blackguards ! " he cried, almost speechless with rage. "You blackguards ! " Then he gave in. Mamie amongst that gang was too terrible to contemplate. Hankey was held while the draft he gave was safely cashed. Then he was quietly dropped ashore. The Greaser did not dare to see Mamie again; but Mr. Hankey, upon his return, left her in no doubt as to the fact that Mr. Eduard Rising and Mr. Howard T. Egerton were one and the same man.
That night she cried herself to sleep for the sake of a man who, whatever he had been to others, was to her a gentleman.

When these details had been carried out the members of the League reassembled in Paris to discuss a coup the One-eyed Man had arranged. "Gentlemen," he said, "-I have a big thing on hand. Can you hazard a guess?" "The stuff from the old galleon, Boss," said the Greaser. "Better game. One-eyed Man. "The Crown _jewels, Boss," said Breed _ _ _ _ _
Guess again," replied the

. . "Hardly that,— Bresci. Even we should find those a tough nut. It's the kidnapping of Golightly T. Hankey, the Multi-millionaire, railway magnate, &c., of New York, Chicago, and Buffalo. We should be able to get a hundred thousand dollars out of him easy. We'll hold him aboard the Submarine." Bresci smiled. "What you say goes, Boss. It's a big order. Can we get him?" The One-eyed Man smiled. "Anything in reason we generally get." The Italian made a deprecatory gesture. "I said can we get him because, Boss, the man is unapproachable. He has not even been interviewed, and journalists fix up any- one as a rule." "Started in pork, followed it up with canned goods, then en to rails, didn't he?" queried the Greaser. "That's him," said the One-eyed Man. "Now for the plan. Greaser, you must make the initial move in this. I must be the bait for the fish. He must come to me. It had better be on the South Coast of England— • Brighton, Deal, anywhere round there. Bresci, you go at once and thoroughly over- haul the Submarine and await instructions. You can catch the night boat." The Italian departed after a few brief in- structions, leaving the Greaser and the One. eyed Man together, and long and earnestly they talked matters over. Finally, the scheme was satisfactorily arranged, and they pre- pared to play their respective parts. Golightly T.' Hankey was staying at the Grand Hotel, London; where he had an ex- tensive suite of rooms, and anyone not imme- diately connected with his entourage found admittance to his august presence a matter of considerable difficulty. The Greaser was in no wise nonplussed, and, armed with a forged letter of introduc- tion, ' he essayed the work before him. He presented a letter purporting to be from the .American Embassy, signed by the secretary, and stamped with the crest and seal of the Legation, stating that , Mr. Howard. T. Eger- ton was introduced to the notice of Mr. Golightly T. Hankey by the secretary, and that his business would fully compensate Mr. Golightly T. Hankey's loss of time in accord- ;rig him an •interview. - The letter was open, as it was an intro- ductory note only. ' This letter secured Mr. Howard T. Egerton almost immediate . ad- mittance to the presence of the millionaire, who, seated in a capacious chair' waVed the Greaser to a seat. Holding the letter in his hand, he addressed his visitor: "You are M. Egerton ? " The Greaser bowed. • "And your business?" " I am here, Mr. Hankey, to offer .you the sole rights and patents relating to an inven- tion of my father, w l io, unfortunately a.. cripple, is unable hims to see you and ode- scribe his patent fully. It is an automatic signalling arrangement, electrically worked, and by it errors on the part of a signalman are rendered impossible.' " Humph ! " grunted the millionaire, "I thought as. much. Selling as , usual." "Mr. Hankey," . said the Greaser, "you are, an American like myself. You sell a rail- way system, if need be, in its entirety; I only trade in a smaller way. It's in the American blond to 'deal,' sir." The millionaire laughed. "You've found the joints of my armour, young man. Have you a model here?" "In the grounds of my father's house at Deal, Mr. Hankey, the whole system is laid out upon a track of some eight hundred yards, where the whole thing can be seen and ex- amined. Would it be worth your while to examine it, sir?" The millionaire thought a moment. "I am spending Sunday in Dover. I will come over on Monday, in the afternoon, say, five o'clock. ; Will that suit you? " "My father will be delighted to welcome . you, sir. As I said, but for the fact of his being a cripple he would have been here to- day in my stead." • "Have you offered it elsewhere?" asked Mi. Hankey. "No, sir. We thought of approaching the Grand Trunk or the C.P.R., but awaited the result of this interview." " Good ! " said the other. "Keep it until • I have inspected your working model." After a few commonplace remarks the in- terview ended. The One-eyed Man was hugely delighted with the Greaser's success, and complimented him upon the skill with which he had carried out the opening details of the scheme. Orders were giveii to Bresci with regard to the Sub- marine, and a rendezvous arranged, a little south of Deal, for Monday, at nine p.m., when, all being well, the One-eyed Man would have Golightly T. 'Hankey in his net. At five p.m. . .on Monday afternoon the millionaire drove .up to the house rented in Deal by the Oneleyed Man. He paid and dis- missed his cabman and rang the Bell. The 'door was opened by the Greaser himself. "Sir;" he said, extending a hand to the millionaire, "you are more than welcome. My father awaits foil in the library. Kindly come forward." Suspecting nothing, . the millionaire fol- lowed in the steps of the Greaser, and as he entered the door of the library a towel was flung over his head, his hands seized from be- hind, and Golightly T. Hankey was a prisoner. .. "Keep his eyes covered," said the One. eyed Man, "but open his mouth." After some trouble this was done. Then a powerful drug was forced down the . throat of the unfortunate man, and in a few minute.' he was unconscious. . div.head: COSTUMES OF THE MOMENT.
div.p: THE COSTUMES OF THE MOMENT.

Some of the most fashionable dresses of the day, says the Qucen, are a mixture of cloth and silk, the cloth being the gown, the silk the trim- ming and the outdoor jacket. There is certainly a ()Teat penchant this year for a mixture of two materials in one costume. I3odices and skirts <-ro together, unless, as so, often happens, the bodice is supplanted by a lace blouse, or one of muslin covered With embroidery, the silk coat being of the same colour as the cloth, and it is in them that the novelty lies. Hardly ever does the sleeve come below the elbow; very often it ends be- tween the elbow and the shoulder, and the back of the jacket or the front rarely reaches to the waist. Some open with revers; some have brace over the shoulders, through which the buckle ,passes on the bust, and below this fall two ends to the waist, tipped with tassels; some have kilted fronts; the majority are bordered with some sort of galon. The tailor gown of the moment is somewhat elaborate, velvet bands as well as braid figuring on many of them. There are light materials, especially black and white. which are now tackled by the tailor, and voile costumes are also corning within his ken. The colours are not so varied as one might think; but, though pink and red and blue are still worn, the tones are very different from those of last year.

div.head: USEFUL SUMMER TUNIC.
div.p: USEFUL SUMMER TUNIC.

A little tunic for knockabout summer wear is the subject of our sketch. It could be suCcess- fully carried out in any strong washing material or a light thin summer serge. Linen, drill, and galatea would all wash admirably, and would all be cool, practical wear for the hot weather. The overall is made with a box-pleat down the middle of the front, flanked on either side with a

wide tuck, being machined firmly near the edges. On either side of the front COMO inverted pleats, machined at the edges and released jus;- below the belt. At the neck turns back a wide sailor collar of white linen or drill, a silk hand- kerchief being folded underneath and knotted in front. The open space in front is filled in by a plain vest of the same material as the collar, headed by a stitched band. Small bishop sleeves finished with turn-back cuffs complete the pretty little tunic. div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Pritnitive Methodist Centenary.

On Sunday afternoon the congregation of Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church held a centenary camp meeting. A procession of scholars and friends was formed at the Sunday school, headed by the Legh-street brass band. Invitations were given at several places in the Bewsey district, after which a meeting was held on the waste ground near,Bewsey Bridge. The Rev. C. L. Stowe presided and the other speakers were Messrs. Whitley and Faulkner, both of whom attended the Mow Cop celebrations. The Legh-street band accompanied the singing of the hymns. _ _

At the eVening service at Legh-street Church, after a brief evangelistic address from the minister itn old- fashioned Love Feast Nras held, a great number of men and women rising to give their testimony. Some of the old-time hymns were sung and the meeting con- tinued until nine o'clock.

div.head: Free Church Council Open-Air Service.
div.p: Free Church Council Open-Air Service.

The first of a series of open-air services under the auspices of the Warrington Free Church Council was held on Sunday evening opposite the Market Hall, Corporation-street. The weather was fine but cold, 1 and when the meeting commenced there was only a small ! attendance, but the numbers increased rapidiy as the I Legh-street Band played the opening hymn. Shortly i afterwards the Salvation Army Band appeared on the scene, bringing with them a large following, and when I they had taken up their position an inspiring scene was I presented. Mr. E. J. Guest presided in the absence of Mr. C. E. Parker, and among others present were the Revs. J. F. Matthews, C. Harvey Cook, J. S. Hughes, i and C. L. Stowe, and Messrs. J. %V. Hayward, Isaacs I Johnson, and J. Bailey. The first address was elivered by the Rev. C. L. Stowe who made a vigorous appeal to the crowd. When a minister left a town,he said, hewas frequently remem- bered liSr the stress he had been in the habit of laying • upon some particular phase of truth. Some had left many practical messages ringing in their ears with reference to their homes and their national duties He would like to emphasise, like the prophet of old, the teaching that however low they might have fallen there ' was still a spark of conscience left within them which if guarded nright would burst into flame and lead them to higher lives. They would, perhaps not have anything to do with Salvation Armies and churches, but if a collection was made in any of the works with which • they were connected on behalf of a poor fellow who had met with an accident, he was sure they would put their hands in their pockets and do all they could for him. A soft place was therefore still left in their hearts and they might, if they would, become better men and nobler women.

The Rev. J. P. MATTnsws said it wosalways pleasant to speak to men in the open air, and he believed in using the public squares whether in propagating secularism, politics, science, or religion. There were many people who never went to church, and he was not disposed to blame them when he came to look at soma of the parsons and the churches. The pulpit had been too far away from the peopls in the past. There . had not been enough of the salt of common sense among the poisons. Perhaps it had been because they bad not been near enough to the heart of the man who wore the fustian. But that state of things was, he was thankful to say, being altered. A man who read the New Testament with his eyes open and his brain clear, and dared to ask his strongest questions, would find satis- factory answers : if the New Testament did not altogether solve his doubts it would soften many of his difficulties, and make him purer, braverand a truer man, and one who would not mind gibes and sneers when he had to stand alone. The keynote of the Gospel was life. Who was the man who lived the best life and understood what the secret of life really was at its finest and best ?—He who companioned with the Master day by clay in all things and at all times. He was sure that if he did so he would grow in sympathy, charm, goodness, strength, sweetness, and hate of that which was gross and wrong.

div.head: Bold-street Church. Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Bold-street Church. Sunday School Anniversary.

Special services were held at Bold-street Wesleynn Church on Sunday in celebration of the anniversary of the Sunday school. Throughout the day these were well attended and the proceedings were in every way highly success- ful. In the morning and evening the pulpit was occugied by the Rey. Percy Ainsworth (Manchester), who delivered powerful and interesting addresses. At each service a special feature was made of the music, the singing of the scholars in a number of hymns being especially pleasing. lhe choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Frank Hickman were heard to great advantage in the anthems "Jerusalem the Golden " and "Abide with Me" and the solos "Entreat me not to leave

thee" and "The voice of the Father "were finely sung by Miss E. Taylor and Mrs. A. Booth. An orchestral band was in attendance and accomplished some excellent work. A flower service was held in the afternoon, at which the proceedings were of a bright and plesing character. Special hymns were sung by the scholars, together with the anthem "Sweet is Thy mercy." Miss Jessie Wood- land gave an excellent rendering of the solo "The songs that the children sing," and 111 r. A. Bates was highly successful in the violin solo "girchen Aria" (Stradella). Mr. H. Plumpton sang with effect "Behold, I stand at the door" Jude).

Alderman FORSHAW presided and said it had been a great pleasure to him to witness the procession of children with their beautiful flowers, which they bad just deposited in the church, and to have heard such excellent singing. A word of praise was certainly due to the choirmaster and conductor (Mr. Frank Hickman) who must have been put to considerable trouble to get up such a charming service. There was no doubt that services of this character ought to receive the hearty support of all Christian people, because they tended to cultivate, elevate, and purify the young mind. To parents these gatherings woo most important, as he believed in the words of the old Book, "Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it." For those services had a tendency to encourage the young to'• worship God in spirit and in truth."
Mr. J. C. B. PERCY, of Manchester, delivered an address on flowers and their cultivation from which he drew excellent moral lessons, giving some very valuable advice to the children.
The collections for the day amounted to about £33.

div.head: Peace Conference.
div.p: The Peace Conference.
Sermon by the Rev. John Yonge,
The Churches and War Fever

"The Master's Benediction of peace" was the subject of the Rev. John Yonge's sermon at Wycliffe Church oil Sunday evening and he took for his text the words "Peace be unto you." He said they should not be unmindful of the great truth that this benediction of peace was really what Christ was saying to the whole world, not only in the spiritual but in -the widest and most actual and all-inclusive sense. The message of the Saviour, who was the Prince of Peace and the King of Kings, concerned the whole world and would bring harmony and concord and tranquillity everywhere and always. It would settle for ever the questions to be discussed this month in the great international Peace Conference at the Hague. It might he a profitable thing for them to be reminded that the Church of Jesus Christ was intended by Him to live and labour for the universal peace and welfare of mankind. The ceparation which had been set up for centuries between the Church and the temporal welfare of the world was an unlawful separation. Jesus of Nazareth made no such separation He cared for the physical and social conditions of humanity as well as for its moral and spiritual, and He Imeant that, His Saints, His followers, should even become the judges and the rulers of the world. Had His people not absointely miaunderstood Hitn,the world's millenium wauld have bean here by now. A remarkable thing was on the eve of happening, and it was this. A Conference, representing all nations, was about to assemble to discuss the peace of the world. The previ- ous conference was only partially representative ; othis, he understood, included all. The strangest and even saddest feature of the case was that the Churches of the Prince of Peace,the Lord and Giver of Peace,had had no hand and had given next to no help in promoting this supremely Christian event. Mr. W. T. Stead, whom some had regarded as an extremist and a visionary, and even a meddlesome and dangerous person, had devoted his life, his intellect, his means, to promoting national and international policies of humanity and peace all over the world. By an energy and courage alike unztralleled and indomit- able, he had been received and listened to by all the ruling powers of civilized nations. And he had just returned from a circular tour among the crowned and uncrowned heads of all Christian European and Americim States. What did he say in his pamphlet on Christian unity in its relation to the Hague Confer- ence? He said: ," Nothing saddened me more, in my run round Europe, than to find everywhere among practical politicians an absolute indifference to the influence of the Christian Church on the question of international peace. Some regarded it as hostile, but the general opinion was that it had ceased to exercise any effective control over,the decisions of nations. The Christian Church, no doubt, continues to exist and may exercise a beneficial influence in other spheres of life. But it has withdrawn from all effort to help the human race along the path which leads to international peace. In this matter, while it has a name to live, it seems to be dead." In so far as this was true, it was infinitely sad. We had, unhappily, in the days of the South African war, only too many and forcible illustrations of how the churches failed to check the war fever, and did nothing to hinder a strife which nearly everybody now admitted to have been a deplorable rniatake. Indeed, the wars had been very few in history, certainly in modern history, which had been justified by the verdicts given after the events. What could be more desirat,la then, and what could he more Christian, than that the Conference about•to assemble should consider and devise a scheme hy which v,-ar should become practically preventable? He trusted his hearers would carefully read Mr. Stead's appeal, and that they would help in the formation of a Christian and public opinion in favour of the proposal he submitted. Mr. Stead rejoiced, as they would see, that the National Free Church Council at its recent meeting in Leeds, passed with enthusiasm a resolution calling upon all the Churches in the fellowship, of which that Church was one, to take nBtlce of that approaching Conference. The resolution urged that on the Sunday preceding the meeting of the Conference, special sermons should be preached and prayer offered from every Free Church pulpit in support of the proposal to inter- pose mediation before the breaking out of war, and that the Press be asked to promulgate this proposal. There had been some hope, continued Mr. Yonge, that the Peace Conference would consider the question of dis- armament. That, it was feared, would be found impossible. Surely, however, the proposal of an agree- ment for mediation before resort to war should be well within the bounds of possibility. Put into few words the proposal was—" No war without prior appeal to mediation or inquiry: and no fighting until after the , expiry of 30 days of &trice allowed for the full con- sideration of the question whether it is really imposed upon us as a Christian duty to kill our brother man instead of sending our dispute with him to arbitration." Surely here was ground for arrangement. It created a pause. Nearly all the wars of modern days had been rushed into with a precipitate and cruel haste. The nations were at this hour more or less armed to the teeth. Collision could occur almost within hours from the occurrence of a dispute. The needed thing, and the Christian thing, was the creation of a period of suspension, during which passion could cool and jucigmeet find space for exercise, and so differences ha mitigated and peace be preserved. Was it not a project appealing. for the support of the Clint chea of the Prince of Peace? Should it not he favneired by all who "profess and call them- selvss Christians " ? Why should the world any longer he hurled into strife by the schemes of politicians, by I the chicanery of often an enprincipled newspaper Press - which fattened upon the &Li of war, or by the unintel- ligent and often insane passion which was miscallea patriotism ? Surely it was the mission of the Church of the Redeemer to promote internatioaal peace and concord, as truly as it was its duty to go into all the world and preach the Gospel of the personal peace with God to every creature. The religion of Christ was the religion of humanity.

POLICE COUR,T AND PRISON GATE MISSION. It is difficult to realize what it means to he dis- charged from a gaol. It has been said" that from the moment which precedes the expiration of his penalty the criminal—even the most hardened—is drawn towards ideas of respectability. Crime and its punish- ment, its consequences to himself and his family present themselves to his mind. How shall I live when Igo out ? " rm.; is the question be puts to him- self day and night. The opportunity must be seized by those who work for the reformation of society. This is what the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Diocesan C.E.T.S. aims at. Every week day morn- ing throughoLt the year the Mission Room near Walton Gaol is open. During the past month 631 prisoners on discharge were provided with breakfast, and were offered employment,counsel,&c. The work in the police courts comprised 239 visits during which 1320 persons weie conversed with in the courts and cells, of whom 650 were afterwards visited in their abodes. One hundred and eight pesons were spoken to in the courts and cells at the special request of the magistrates. The court officials and the police also used the missionaries' services on behalf of 63 persons. Ffty women, girls, and boys were taken to homes, provided with work or sent hack to friends. Food and clothing were provided for 87 persons. Many of these had been found employ- ment. Eighty-four persons, who were in danger of prosecution or imprisonment, had the advice and assist- nee of the missionaries. In their efforts at reclatnation and prevention 239 persons were assisted by the!mission- aries, who also wrote no fewer than 222 letters in these efforts. Twenty-one tickets for work at . the Society's Firewood and Mat Factory, Bootle, were gLven to men. In five other instances the loss of employment was averted by the efforts of the missionaries. One hundred and sixty-five persons pledged themselves to abstain from strong drink. Twenty-eight meetings were addressed; &c., &o.

The British net tonnage mounted to 8;290,931, the German to 2,155,552, and the ranch 856,311 tons.

div.head: LAND AND THE WORKS.
div.p: THE LAND AND THE WORKS.

No shackles bind the winds of heaven, No leashes curb the sea; And to mankind the land was given, From every impost free. Unbound as air, where'er he goes, The Arab's tent is spread ; No grasping lord the savage knows, Free nature yields him bread. Bu t in these Isles where Churches rise, And good men sing and pray; How sad to hear oppression's cries Wax louder day by day. Robb/d of their birthright in the soil, In some barbaric age; In grimy works the people toil, For less than "living wage."
No fields are theirs, no meadows green, Not e'en an humble cot; Poor toilers in life's busy scene, How dreary is their lot!

Then 0 how cheerie-ss ire their homes, Bereft of trees and flowers ; Where glorious sunshine never comes, To light the dismal hours. And these are some of Mammon's ways, Which press the toiling poor; That idle men may spend their days In luxury secure. While smooth-tongued preachers preach the while, Bow meekly to the rod; And tell their hearers with a smile, It is the hand of God ! June, 1007. J. H. W. CLINDINNING.

Seventy-five firemen belonging to the North German Lloyd steamer Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse struck just before the vessel sailed from New York on Tuesday,and threatened to prevent her starting, unless they were paid for working overtime. The company paid the amount asked for.

div.p: SHIP CANAL BILL.

div.head: COMPENSATION CLAUSE GRANTED.
div.p: COMPENSATION CLAUSE GRANTED.

After a hearing extending over five days the House of Commons Committee. presided over by Mr. Nussey, on Tuesday gave its decision on the Manchester Ship Canal (Various Powers) Bill, which empowers the Company to pump from the estuary with the object of increasing the supply of water in the upper reaches of the canal. The traders and Corporation of Warrington petitioned for a clause entitling them to compensation in the evelit of the water which finds its way over Woolston Weir into the Mersey being deteriorated for manufacturing purposes by reason of increased salinity. Mr. Balfour Browne, K.C., representing the Canal Company, opposed the granting of this clause. It had been suggested, he said, that the Company might obtain the necessary water from the red sandstone in Man- chester or by the construction of reservoirs fed from the rivers, but no evidebce had been given in support of these suggestions. The only question was whether the proposed pumping of water from the estuary length into the Latchford length would do harm to the traders by increasing the salinity of the water entering the Mersey at Rixton. It was not enough that the Petitioners should have a mere apprehension; they Inust show, in order to entitle them to a clause, that there was a real probability of damage being done. The evidence of Mr. Hunter, Mr. Scudder, Professor Prankland, Sir A. Kennedy, and Sir Douglas Fox was that there would be the greatest difficulty in ascertaining Whether the salinity of the water—already a variable quantity—was due to pumping or to increased lockage, the latter being done in pursuance of the powers the Company already possessed. He spoke of the action brought by the Warrington Corporation in regard to the Walton sluices as a " trick.' The Committee found the preamble of the Bill proved, subject to the insertion of a clause entitling the Warrington petitioners to compensation if it could be shown that any substantial increase in the salinity of the water flowing over Woolston Weir (on the Mersey). E o as to cause material damage ,to the peti- tioners, had been caused by the pumping operations at Latchford Lock.

div.head: TRADERS' PROTECTIOF CLAUSE.
div.p: TRADERS' PROTECTIOF CLAUSE.

The Ship Canal i3ill was finally disposed of by Mr. Nussey's Committee on Wednesday. Rival clauses were brought up by the promoters and by the Corporation and traders of. Warrington, to give effect to the com- mittee's decision that the petitioners against the Bill Should be entitled to compensation if it could be shown that any substantial increase in tne salinity of the water flowing over Woolston Weir, so as to cause material damage to the petitioner's works, had been caused by the pump at Latchford Lock. The clause presented by the t anal Company followed literally the terms of the Committee's decision, while' that of the petitioners sought to extend the right so compensation to all traders, and to provide that in the event of a dispute the amount of the compensation should be determined bY arbitration vnder the Lands Clauses Act. The Committee accepted the promoters' clause, hich, the Chairman said, more neariy carried out the Intentions. The Bill was ordered to be reported for third reading. , TEE COUNCIL AND THE CANAL COMPANY.

,-- - - At a meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday, it 'was reported that the Rivers Committee had resolved that notice be served on the Manchester Ship Canal eumpany of the intention of the Corporation to take °ver the joint coritrel management and direction of the luiees at Walton Lock, and that the Borough Surveyor i.Je appointed to exercise and carry out such joint con- ‘ .t°l, management, and direction at the expense of the company. Alderman BFNNETT, in the absence of the Chairman end Deputy-Chairman, proposed the adoption of the Rivers Committee minutes. He cord ially congratulated the town on the successful result of .the action of the traders against the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and hoped all points at issue between them would soon be deanitely settled, and that they would work in that amicable spirit which so many members of the Council desired. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FULTON-SMITH seconded. The CHAIRMAN said it was reported in that night's evening paper that the Committee of the House of Pornmons had that day passed the Ship Canal Bill, sub- at to a clause providing for compensation to the 'traders of Warrington in the event of their sustaining damage through increased salinity as the result of the Pumping proposed by the Company. (Hear, hear.) That was a very valuable consideration. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were adopted.

The neighbours, becoming alarmed at his long absence, forced an entrance into his house, and ""uPon going upstairs found him lying lifeless on the bed.

div.head: ,iAiihik.
div.p: ,iAiihik.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] MRS. BENTON'S LODGER.
BY ALYS HALLARD.
Author of "Mistaken," "A Silent Tragedy," "An Artist's Story," "Where the Roads Divide," "The Expected Guest," &c.

was certainly not a very inviting locality for triyone with fastidious tastes, the lower end of Tottenham Court-road just near to the gallery entrance to the theatre, but the man who was tow looking at the house from outside seemed quite satisfied with his choice. "You see I have come back to you," he said, as the door opened in answer to his ring. "I thought I should," he added with a smile, taking off his hat as he followed his future landlady into her parlour. "There are just two or three matters I want to speak about," began Mrs. Benton in a business- like tone, as she closed the door and gave her visitor a chair. "My sister and I have been thinking over all you told us, and we are afraid the irregular hours will be very inconvenient to us."

Miss Cragg, a spinster of some forty-five years of age, glanced up from her crochet work and fixed her piercing eyes on the would-be lodger. For fifteen mortal years she had been living with her widowed sister in this dingy house in Tottenham Court-road, and during all these fifteen years she and her sister had disagreed on every subject they had discussed. Mrs. Benton, as a married woman and the possessor of an annuity of twenty-five pounds a-year, talked down to the penniless spinster from a very superior height, while Miss Cragg's sole ambition in life was to prove herself wiser than this very wise sister. Their five-storeyed house was let off in single rooms to homeless men, who, with the exception of their breakfast, took their meals elsewhere or went without, according to the state of their purses. The duel between the two sisters was fought afresh every day of their live. Sometimes the lighting of the kitchen fire at six o'clock in the morning led up to it, . sometimes another apparently trifling incident. On the day in question Mr. Rebbor, the would- be tenant of the vacant room on the ground floor, - had stirred up terrible strife in the domestic camp. Miss Cragg knew perfectly well that the extra work which irregular hours invariably occasion would fall upon her. It was not that she actually objected to work, but she was extremely methodical, and liked to get every- thing done at a certain time each day in order to devote herself to crochet work and embroidery. She had found a warehouse which kept her supplied with orders, and this was her only *ay of making a little extra money towards com- peting with that annuity of her sister's which was such a sore point with her. "You see, we don't keep any servant," con- tinued Mrs. Benton, firmly; "so that all extra work falls on us—on my sister and me." A sarcastic smile flickered over Miss Cragg's thin lips. The widow knew perfectly well what it implied, but she deemed it better policy at that particular moment to feign blindness. "Oh, yes," answered Mr. Rebbor, promptly; "of course, I know that my irregular hours will give you more trouble, and I am quite willing to pay a shilling or two a; week for the extra attend- ance. I don't want you to be inconvenienced any more than is absolutely necessary," he said, apologetically. "All the gentle Men we have here are most regular," went on Mrs. Benton, in a hard, unrelenting way. Her fifteen years' experience had taught her that if a landlady gives an inch her lodger will take more than an ell. "They have their breakfast at the hour they ask for it— and punctualjsir, to the tick of the clock !—and after that their boots, and then out they go till evening. Saturdays and Sundays we see more of them; but meals are all regular, sir, and we never cook for any of them except at, breakfast time and Sunday dinner."

"I should like to tell you something in con- fidence," said Mr. Rebbor, lowering his voice instinctively. Miss Cragg looked up from her crochet and positively wasted time. Life was so monotonous in their dingy house.that any little mystery was most welcome.
"Of course, I must ask you to be careful not to speak to anyone of what 1 am going to toll you, as the slightest... indiscretion might be so disastrous.

"We are not given to talking," observed Mrs. Bentoß, in a dignified way. "No, I felt sure of that, and I may add that I came back to you now on that account. You see, I cannot live in a house where there is a servant —my profession is one which makes it very difficult for me to get suitable rooms." . _

' There was silerice for a few seconds in the little dark parlour. The two women were aching with curiosity, and Mr. Rebbor was evidently hesitating about the advisability of imparting his grave secret to these two strangers. "I may trust you, mayn't 1? " he said at length, looking from Mrs. Benton to her sister. "You can trust us, sir," answered the widow, drawing herself up proudly. "We are Scotch- women, and if you know anything of the Scotch you must be aware that horses wouldn't drag a word out of them that they didn't want to say. I can keep a secret, sir, and as for my sister— well, she's the stubbornest creature that ever walked the eaith." Mrs. Benton felt relieved when she had uttered this speech, and she flattered herself that she had very cleverly killed two birds with one stone. "Well, then," said Mr. Rebbor, again dropping his voice, "the fact is I am a private detective. "A private detective ?." echoed Mrs. Benton, aghast. "Yes," continued her new lodger, "and I am obliged to have a room that is 'quite central where I can just get a few hours' sleep when I have time. My work, of course, takes me out a great deal, and when I have a case on that I am following up you must be prepared for allkinds of vagaries. "Vagaries ? " repeated Mrs. Benton, who felt she should like to_know at any rate what she had to expect.

"Yes," said Mr. Rebbor, calmly, rather enjoying the sensation he was causing. "I am frequently obliged to disguise myself, for instance. You will see me one day appear as a workman, another day I shall look like a millionaire going out to his club; you may see me sometimes wearing a clerical get-up--" "But what about my other lodgers, sir; they'll wonder whether I've got a madman in the house." "Not at all; if they once see me as I am now they will never recognise the other individuals they may meet going in or out of my room. You may just give it out that I am a lawyer, and they will conclude that_ the strange people they meet are my clients." "Excuse me' sir, I can't give out any lies. I'm a. truthful woman and a Presbyterian.' "I should not ask you to give out lies," replied Mr. Rebbor, somewhat. haughtily. "I am a lawyer, and when I have had enough of this detective business I shall return to my profession. Of course," he added, in a dignified manner, "if you do not care to let your room to me I will go and search elsewhere. After all, lam not very difficult to suit; all I require is a ground-floor bedroom in a house where there is no servant kept, and I am always willing to pay for any extra trouble I may give. Well, I won't detain you, ladies," and the wily detective bowed as though to take leave. "I don't see any objection, after all,' remarked Mrs. Benton, in a lingering way. She was evidently talking to her own conscience, for her sister appeared to be entirely absorbed in her crochet work.

"Oh, if you have any scruples don't hesitate for a moment," suggested Mr. Rebbor, whose dealings with women had taught him the value of "contrariwise" argument. "No, I don't see that there's any need to have scruples," answered Mrs. Benton. 'After all, 'one trade's as good as another, and as long as there's so much wickedness in the world we must have police and detectives--" " Yes, " continued Mr. Rebbor, foil owing promptly the worthy Scotchwoman's lead; "and the police and detectives, being human, must have a roof to shelter them and food to eat. You have no idea how hard our life is," he added, with a resigned simile. Miss Cragg looked up for a minute from her work, glanced at the new lodger, then at her sister, and, pursing up her lips, proceeded to. crochet as though her very life depended on getting the round she had commenced finished at a certain moment.
"There is only one thing I must ask you," began Mr. Rebbor again. "and that is to be very

careful not to give any information whatever to inyone who may come here asking questions shout me. I will tell you in confidence, so that, you may avoid any unpleasantness later on, it is very possible that people will be sent here: perhaps a police inspector may come and put all !ands of questions to you. You must be on you' ..zuard, and not give any information whatever, exeept that I am a lawyer, and that I have come here from Manthester. Such disastrous things !night happen through the indiscretion of my landlady that when I change my address the "%teotland Yard people sometimes send round to test for themselves whether I have chosen wisely. [am only telling you this so that you may' be on your guard." "As I said before, sir, horses wouldn't drag a ‘vord out of a Seotchwoman when she doesn't intend to speak." . "Well, then, I'll just go and fetch my luggage and take possession of my rood at once," said Mr. Rebbor.

"I only hope nothing unpleasant will happen," remarked Miss Cragg a few minutes later, when her sister returned to the parlour after closing the hall door for the new lodger. "That room's been to let three weeks, and :7" one likes the ground-floor," answered Mrs. Benton, sharply. "Would you have had ma refuse a good offer—two shillings a week more than we've ever had for it ? "

"Oh, my opinion wasn't asked before the matter was settled, it's of no use asking me now that the man's in the house, as you may say. I only hope nothing unpleasant will happen," and Miss Cragg shook her head gravely and continued her crochet work.

There was no more monotony for the two sisters in their dingy house in Tottenham Court- road. The irregular habits of the downstairs lodger and his clever disguises kept their minds fully occupied. Then, too, he was extremely agreeable, and on the rare occasions when he had time for a chat he would regale them with thrilling dories of burglaries and murders in Manchester. Sometimes for his disguises he had recourse to Mrs. Benton or to Miss Cra,gg for a faw necessary stitches, and as he was most liberal with compensation for all services rendered, both sisters were always willing to help him.

"It is, as you may say, a service that we are doing the country," remarked Mrs. Benton one day as she was mending the buttonhole of one of Mr. Rebbor's clerieal collars. "Without these private detectives I suppose we should simply bc overrun with thieves and vagabonds of all kinds." "I wonder what he's going to be up to, dis- guised as a curate ? " said her sister. "I'll venture to say he's going to do more good than the Papists disguised as curates in the Ritualist churches here."

"I only hope, as I've said before, that nothing unpleasant will happen," remarked Miss Cragg, solemnly. "Yes, you've said that a good many times lately. It's a pity you can't find something fresh to say," retorted Mrs. Benton, cutting her cotton with more energy than was necessary. Miss Cragg maintained a dignified silence after this rebuff, and in her inmost soul longed for some- thing very unpleasant to happen in connection with the new lodger.

A few days later there was great excitement in the neighbourhood. The jewellery shop opposite to Mrs. Benton's had been broken into during the night, and so cleverly was the robbery effected that no trace of the thieves was to be found. Mr. Rebbor went across to look at the premises, and returned in a great state of excitement and disgust. "Just to think that my window faces the shop, and that I had such a fine opportunity or seeing the whole thing through, and I was miles away trying to track another affair," he said, when Mrs. Benton came into his room with his break- fast tray. "Yes, it does seem a pity, sir; but no doubt Providence was watching over you. If you had gone out alone, and there had been two or three burglars, you might have been a dead man, sir, now." _ _

"Instead of a very hungry one, ready for breakfast," he said, laughing. Mrs. Benton stayed some little time chatting with her lodger. She told him what the neigh- bours said about the burglary, and be repeated to her some of the remarks he had heard from the people in the street, who were gazing at the shop window when he had gone across himself to look round. Within the next fortnight three more daring robberies were effected from jewellers' shops in Oxford-street. The third one caused a great sensatibn, as it wti,S very evident that he thieves had entered the establishment with a key, taken all they wanted, and walked quietly away. A diamond and pearl necklace of great value was among the articles missing. It was a neck- lace which had ;..t,racted great attention at the Paris Exhibition. The French jeweller had arranged to lend it as an advertisement to this London house, and it had been on view in the window for more than a month. A large reward was offered to anyone who should give such information as would lead to the recovery Of this valuable necklace.

- "A line lot of use it is to have policemen and private detectives," observed Miss Crag to her sister as she was peeling the potatoes for dinner; "roar burglaries in a fortnight, all in the same neighbourhood, and all the thieves at large ! " "Policemen and private detectives are human beings," replied Mrs. Benton; "they can't be in a dozen different places at once. There's only God Almighty that can put a stop to the wicked- ness in this world, and that'll be by putting a stop to the world itself, I'm thinking." Mr. Rebbor had been retailing to the Seotchwoman a story of the most gruesome kind; and she had not recovered from the horror of it. The detec- tive had quickly noted the antagonism between the two sisters, and, although he was always extremely polite to both of them he certainly, talked more to the widow than to her sister, thereby rousing the jealousy of the latter. "They get their money easily enough, anyhow, these private detectives," continued Miss Cragg. "That man's been in bed all this morning, and alter dinner I suppose he'll smoke and read the papers until tea-time, as he did yesterday." "He's got a case on that he has to be ready for at any moment," remarked Mrs. Benton, proud of her superior knowledge. "While he is hanging about doing nothing I should think he might help to track these mid- night burglars." "He's doing that," observed the widow; "he's on the track of the one that stole the diamond neck/ace. He told me this morning that the man who walked into that shop so coolly has committed at least a dozen of the most daring robberies, but so far he's been one too}nany for the polio." "If Mr. Rebbor knows NN ho it is, (why doesn't he have him arrested ? "

"He's biding his time, and waiting to catch him in his next robbery. You see' you can't walk into a man's house and arrest him when he's sitting at his tablo drinking a cup of tea if you haven't any proofs that he is guilty; you've got to have something definite to go on."
"You seem to know a great deal about the ;aw," remarked Miss Cragg, sarcastically. "We shlll have you setting up for a female detective next."

"I daresay I could get my liding at that, if I wanted to," retorted Mrs. Banton. "Nobody has over yet been able to take me in and I can put two and two together better than certain people I know." Miss Cragg understood the allusion and was silent. She had once, in a weak moment, lent ten shillings to a lodger, who had never repaid her, and who had gone away leaving no address. That afternoon Mr. Rebbor rang for, tea an hour earlier than usual. Miss Cragg was annoyed, as she always reckoned on two clear hours for her crerehet work before getting tea. "You're earlier, sir, to-day," she said, as she set the tray down on the table, and there was a world of meaning in the simple remark. "Yes, I'm sorry if I've inconvenienced you,r answered the detective, who was not an obtuse man, "but the fact is I've smoked my throat dry and finished reading all the news," and he pointed to a whole pile of papers on the sofa. "Oh, I think I'll just go to the corner of the greet and get something else to read while I'm having tea," he continued, getting up hastily and going cut of the room, while Miss Cragg spread a cloth across the end of the table and arranged the tea-things. AL she passed by Mr. Itbbor's trunk the key caught in her dress, and, -is she had never before seen the key left in the lock, she took the opportunity of opening the lid quickly, just to see how this lodger kept hiit things. The tray was full of cardboard boxes, and she opened the largest one: but so great was her

astonishment at what she saw inside that she started back and instinctirely looked round the room. She bent down again and examined carefully tho contents of this box, opened two or three others, and then closed the trunk, turned the key, and retired to the kitchen. A few minutes later she heard Mr. Rebbor's latch-key in the lock of the hall door, and as soon as he had gone into his own room Miss Cragg went upstairs and put on her bonnet and cloak. Mrs. Benton was in her bedroom changing her dress, snd was surprised to see her sister with her bonnet on.

"I'm going to take my crochet," explained Miss Cragg. "Mr. Rebbor rang for his tea an hour too early, and that disturbed me. The kettle is on for our tea, and I shall be back very soon." Mrs. Benton did not vouchsafe any answer, and Miss Cragg went out by the entry door. More than an hour later, just as the widow had finished her third cup of tea, Miss Cragg walked into the kitchen and sat down as though exhausted.

"The tea's bitter with standing," remarked M.S. Benton, in a complacent tone. "I don't care about the tea," gasped Miss Cragg. "Why, you've never shut the hall door . . . there's somebody coming in!" exclaimed Mrs.l Benton, on hearing footsteps in the hall. "Yes—three men—they've come with me in all four-wheeler," said Miss Cragg, with a frantic effort to control her voice and.' appear calm. "Three men!" repeated Mrs. Benton, at th same time walking quickly to the kitchen door and flinging it open, just in time to see three men entering Mr. Rebbor's room. "What fool's trick have you been up to ? " she exclaimed, turning to her sister in a fury. "Some folks are not as wise as they imagine themselves," remarked Miss Cragg. sarcastically; "nor so clever at putting two and two together as they fancy they are." "Are you going to explain what this means or, not ? " demanded Mrs. Benton, ignoring the sarcasm.
"It means that at Scotland Yard Mr. Rebbor is not known, and that it seems as though I have put them on the track of a burglar they've wanted for some time."

"Nonsense!" exclaimed Mrs. Benton, who would believe in anything rather than the per- spicacity of her spinster sister. "We shall see whether it's nonsense when these men from Scotland Yard have looked into our lodger's trunk." "And have you looked into it ? " asked Mrs. Benton, her curiosity overcoming all other. senti- ments.
"I have," answered Miss Cragg, pursing up her liys.in.her most aggravating way.
"Well ? "The diamond necklace is in it—the diamond necklace for which the big reward is offered." "Good Heavens ! " exclaimed Mrs. Benton. _

"There 7;1; ia-o-x-e-s and boxes of jewellery, and there are revolvers enough to kill all of us," went on Miss Cragg, revelling in the sensation she was causing.. "I can't help feeling thankful that I wasn't taken in with the wretch and that I haven't made a friend of him as you have." Mrs. Benton did not wait for any more of her sister's eloquence. She crossed the narrow hall, and opening the door of Mr. Rebbor's room discovered her lodger handcuffed. "Ah, Mrs. Benton," he exclaimed, "see how the mighty are fallen. I shan't be able to enter- tain you any more with my nice little blood- curdling stories. I must thank you for the hospitality you have given me in your house, it is so well situated and coevenient in every way that, upon my word, lam sorry to leave it. You see, there is an entry and a hall door; then it is just opposite the jeweller's there," he con- tinued, nodding towards the window. "Why, if only I could have been left undisturbed I should have made enough money for the rest of my life, and I should have shaken the dust of London from my boots and ended my days in a sunnier clime."
Mrs. Benton was looking at him in amazement and horror.

"Just let the lady see the beautiful diamond necklace which tempted me," he began again, turning to one of the detectives, who was over- hauling the cardboard boxes in the trunk. The man smiled, and lifting the lid of the largest box exhibited the magnificent necklace. "A beautiful piece of workmanship," remarked Mr. Rebbor. "You see, I could not resist it." "And to think that I've been harbouring you here!" exclaimed Mrs. Benton, getting back her voice at last.

"Yes, it is strange that -people are so easily duped," remarked her ex-lodger. "Just to think now that yea had only to spell my name back- wards and you might have known whom you were taking into your house. R-o-b-b-e-r—and yet you never took that tip when I gave it you. The only thing I regret in the whole affair, Mrs. Benton, is that it is your lynx-eyed sister who will pick up the reward. Now I wish, at any rate, it could be divided, and•you may count on uie for using all my influence on your behalf—" "Now then, we are ready," interrupted one of the police-officers, who had been talking in a low voice to his companions. "Then we shall have to say good-bye," remarked Mr. Rebbor with a smile to Mrs. Benton. "Give my kind regards to your sister, as she does not put in an appearance," he added, "and tell her that if ever I should be free again I will search her out and call on her to thank her for the service she has rendered me."

Miss Cragg, standing in the hall, heard these words, and rushed trenibling into the kitchen, where she remained until the prisoner had driven away with his two escorts. The third police-officer then went to the window, and on making a sign a cart which was standing on the other side of the road drove across to the door and another policeman in plain clothes stepped out. The prisoner's luggage was all collected and placed on the vehicle, and the two men in charge drove away with it. "I thought you said you were going to take your crochet," remarked Mrs. Benton, sarcasti- cally, to her sister, who was just making herself some fresh tea. Miss Cragg professed great piety, so that there was some satisfaction, at any rate in catching her in a deliberate lie. "I took my crochet with me," answered the wily spinster, triumphantly. "There it is," she added, pointing to a brown-paper parcel on the table. hadn't time to go to the warehouse with it, though. But I don't much mind, .as this reward will pay me better for my afternoon's work than all the crochet I could do in a year or two."
"Just to think what we've been harbouring in this house!" said Mrs. Benton.
"My opinion was not asked when he man came here," observed her sister, drily, and I always said I hoped nothing unpleasant would happar. [THE END. 1

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 8, 1907.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 8, 1907.
BREACH OF THE FACTORY ACT.

At Runcorn, on Monday, Unsworth Brothers, High- street, tailors and outfitters, were summoned on six informations by Mr. Shinner, inspector of factories and workshops, for working young girls after the legal period. Mr. Jabez Unsworth represented the firm and pleaded guilty. Inspector Sedgwick said the girls were working at 8.35 p.m. on the • 4th May. Mr. Unsworth saki he was away at the time, and the forewoman, who had only been with him a fortnight, kept the girls at work without his knowledge and consent. A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed in each case; total, .£3 Gs.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
DEPUTATION EXPENSES.

The monthly meeting of the Town Connell was held on Tuesday evening, Alderman Pierpoint being voted to the chair in the absence of the Mayor and Deputy Mayor. There were also present :—Aldermen A.Bennett, John Evans, W. J. Forshaw, D. Tinnion, Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, J. Ball, W. Benson, T. Burton, T. Chantler, W. Clegg, E. Cunnington, D. S. Duncan James Evans, L. Ellison, J. Hawthorn, Dr. Joseph, Lord, J. J. Neild, J. Pemberton, J. Sankey, J. Skelland,T. S. Steel, .1. Fulton-Smith, F. Stott, 0. Toole, G. T. Wilding, J. Wilkinson, W.. 1. Wilson, A. T. Hallawny (deputy town (clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), F. V. L. Mathias (electrical engineer),J. M. Murray (director of education). • MANAGER FOR HAMILTON-STREET SCHOOL. Councillor FULTON-SMITH proposed that Councillor Stott be appointed a representative manager of the Hamilton-street School in place of the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, resigned. Councillor WILKINSON seconded, and the preposition was adopted. DEPUTATION EXPENSES. COUNCILLOR STOTT'S CRITICISMS.

Councillor STOTT moved :—" That a return of all expenses paid to, or on behalf of each member of the Council for serving on deputations,&c., be prepared and presented to the Council, together with information as to the purpose for which they were incurred, such return , to cover a period of thrte years ending May 315t,1907." He said he submitted the motion for several reasons. One was because that for some time there had been considerable dissatisfaction, not Only in the Council, but outside, and numerous complaints had been made with reference to the expenses of certain members of the Council so far as deputations were concerned, and also as to the methods of appointing deputations. It had been asserted that members of the Council were making a good thing out of their positions as public representatives. In order to bring the matter to a head he thought the best course to adopt was to submit a definite motion to test the feeling as to whether the members were satisfied with the present condition of things and also to give them an opportunik+ of stating their grievance and bringing forward evidence to show that it was necessary a change should take place. He made no charge of extravagance against any individual member or against the Council collectively. He found that at the last meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee an account was passed for expenses incurred by the Mayor for a journey to London for seven days amounting to £l7 7s. Another account was passed in connection with the expenses of the Town Clerk for nine days in London at a cost of £l7. When they took into consideration the fact that the Town Clerk was also paid his salary for the time being they were indebted to the Town Clerk to the extent of £37. That sum was more than hundreds of families in Warrington had had to live upon diving the past ten months. He did not know whether the deputations were paid at trade union rates or whether they received double pay for Sun- day or for the whole of the day on which they started and for the day on which they came back, nor did he know whether a scale of charges existed. He had often heard trade union officials on deputations condemnel for battening on the working classes for 10s. 6.1. a day, but apparently there were others who knew how to batten on the working classes. Then there was another complaint, and that was that only certain members of the Council stood any chance of being appointed on deputations—that the positions were monopolized by a handful of members. It might be argued—and there was a good deal of truth in it—that certain members possessed special ability. in fact that they were to some extent rather experts. If they wanted to purchase a stack of hay or a horse the Council would do wisely to select Councillor Evans or Councillor Sankey in preference to a man like himself. who would not know which way to put a collar on a horse or tell wheat straw from oat straw. There were also complaints that the custom was to select the chair- men of committees for deputations. It might be argued that chairmen were men of much greater experience than the ordinary members of the committee. That might be true if they selected the beat men on the Council as chairmen but the honour was generally con- ferred for long service. His experience had been that when men were appointed to attend conferencer on behalf of the organizations which appointed them the members of the organizations received an epitome of the business which was supposed to come up for discus- sion at the conference and the deputations were advised how to act so that they might be able to voice the opinions pf the men they were supposed to represent. (Hear, hear). Recently the Mayor and the Town Clerk were sent to London to attend the annual meeting of the ASsociation of Municipal Corporations. He expected an agenda would have been sent to the mem- bers of the Council relating to the business to be trans- acted, but he had no knowledge of any agenda having been brought before tbe Council nor did he know that the two gentlemen approached the Council for advice. Nor had any report been presented by the two repre- seatatives named as to the business of the meeting. An account had been presented and pressed to the extent of about £2O. He strongly objected to the principle of certain men and officials being appointed to represent them and thought gentlemen appointed ought to secure the opinion of the majority of the members of the Council or they could not properly represent the Council. He hoped the resolution mould be passed and that in the future all cause of complaint would de done away with. Councillor LORD seconded and the motion was approved by twelve votes to ten. THE NEW MEDICAL OFFICER.

The committee, at a meeting held on May 15, resolved that Dr. J. Coate Hibbert, assistant medical officer of health, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, be appointed Medical Officer of Health for the borough at a salary of £4.10 per annum, subject to the conditions of appointment approved by the Council. Councillor EVANS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he was sorry to have to inform the Council that Dr. Gaffilan, the acting medical officer of health, was ill, and as a result the Health Committee were rather badly fixed. Dr. Fox had kindly undertaken the duties at the hospital, and there was no cause what- ever for any uneasiness on the part of the members of the Council. He hoped that Dr. Gaffikin would soon be better. (Hear, hear). Councillor Butrros seconded, and the motion was carried. CHEAPER BATHING FACILITIES.

Councillor STorr asked the Chairman of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee :- 1. Whether the committee have yet taken steps to carry out, the resolution of the Council of December 46, 1906, in reference to the provision of additional and cheaper bathing facilities.
2. When will the- co-nmittee be prepnred to present scheme for the consideration of the Council?

3. Have the committee yet considered the provision of an open-air bath for the Orford-lane Recreation Ground in accordance with the resolution of the Council of the 23th October, 1904? The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK replied with reference to questions 1 and 2 that a report was in preparation and vroold shortly be laid before the Council. With reference to the third question, he had to report that a special sub-committee had recently been appointed to deel with the matter, and that a report would shortly be laid before the Council.

SECONDARY SCHOOL AND THE GYMNASIUM. At a meeting of the Gymnasium Committee, hold on May Bth, a deputation from the School Management Committee, consisting of Councillor Fulton-Smith, the Rev. Canon Stevenson, Mr. C. E. Parker, and the Director of Education, waited upon the Committee with reference to the use of the Gymnasium by the Secondary School scholars as an assembly room. The deputation were informed that the Committee were prepared to agree to the Gymnasium being used as suggested sub- ject to satisfactory working arrangements being made, the same to be discussed at a further meeting to be held, and it was resolved that the School Management Committee be offered the use of the Gymnasium as above stated, for the sum of £2OO per annum. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Alderman TINNION, seconded by Councillor CLF.G G.

ELECTRICITY AND TRAMWAYS COMNIITTEE. A meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee was held on the Bth May. when it was resolved that the tender of Nfessrs. McDowell, Ltd., for six tramcar covers at £B5 each be accepted, subject to the terms of an agreement to be prepared by the Town Clerk. _ _ _

The TOWN CLERK reported that the London and North-Weitern Railway Company had limited the power of their Bill now before Parliament with regard to the working of their railway by electrical power to the railways and widenings to be authorized by the Bill in the counties of Loudon, Middlesex and Hertford. The minutes were passed on the proposition of Coun- cillor WILKINSON, seconded by Dr. JOSEPH. DEPUTATION TO BLACKPOOL.

The Fire Engine Committee, at their meeting on May 27th,resolved that the Chairman, Mr.Councillor Burton, and the Superintendent, with siz members of the brigade, be appointed to attend the annual demonstra- tion of the Lancashire Fire Brigades Friendly Society at Blackpool on the Ist June, and that each member of the brigade' be allowed 7s. 6d. for expenses in addition to railway fare. Also that the Chairman or Deputy- Chairman and the Superintendent be appointed to attend the annual meeting of the Association of Profes- sional Fire Brigade o.:ficors to be held in Liverpool on the 12th and 13th June next. _ - -

The minutes having been proposed by Councillor BURTON, and seconded, Councillor CHAN-mut remarked, amid laughter, that the deputation had been to Blackpool before the resolu- tion had been passed by the Council. Councillor BwrroN deicribed the visit and said they had a special invitation from the Mayor of Blackpool to have lunch with him. He (Councillor Burton) thought that was very nice, and he would, if possible,

like an open letter sent to the Mayor of Blackpool expressing their gratitnde for his kind hospitality. The CHAIRMAN: lam sure the Council will have no objection to your doing that. (Laughter). Councillor BURTON added that the men sent from Warrington compared favourably with any of the fire- men who took part in the procession. The minutes were carried.
WARRINGTON BRIDGE. SCHEME FOR A NEW STRUCTURE.

Councillor STOTT asked the Chairman of the General Purposes Committee :- 1. Whether the proposed widening of Warrington Bridge, and the provision of a bridge over the Mersey at Howley have been abandoned? The CHAIRMAN replied on behalf of the Mayor as follows :- 1. No.
2. The scheme for widening Warrington Bridge, or rather the erection of a new bridge at Bridge Foot is practically complete, and full details will be placed before the Council at an early date.

div.head: PROPERTY OWNERS PLEASED.
div.p: PROPERTY OWNERS PLEASED.

The following letter from the Warrington Property Owners' Association was read at a 'meeting of the General Purposes Committee :—" Warrington, May 6th 1907. The members of the Warrington Town Council. Gentlemen,—We desire to compliment you on the successful year's working which has enabled you to reduce the rates of the borough 4d. in the £, and as property owners we fully appreciate this, although our educational rate tends upwards (to meet which few, if any, owners increased their rents). We have on some occasions differed from you on certain schemes, still with yourselves, we have but one aim in view, namely, the prosperity of the town. Hoping that you may still be able to make further reductions and thereby induce manufacturers to erect works in the district,—We remain, yours faithfully. Wa.rington and District Property Owners' Association, R. W. COOK, Secretary." Alderman BFmarrr, expressed the satisfaction with which he read the letter from the Property Owners' Association. It was an unusual experience for the Council to be complimented by outside institutions, and he thought at last they were endeayourin4 to do the Town Council justice.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF PROFESSIONAL AUDITORS.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF PROFESSIONAL AUDITORS.
THE AUDIT ON' ACCOUNTS. ALDERMAN BENNETT AND NEWSPAPER CRITICISM.

Alderman BENNETT said he was sorry to see in one of their leading local papers a paragraph reflecting upon the stability of the Corporation accounts quoted from the official organ of the chartered accountants, calcu- lated to convey a wrong impression to the public, and he thought it was his duty to try to put the matter right. The paragraph insinuated that had a professional auditor been appointed the recent reduetion of the rates would not have been practicable. The accounts of the town, so far as he was aware, were kept as well as those of any town in the United Kingdom. He was satisfied that the town ought to have its accounts audited by a pro- fessional acconotant, but there were two reasons why it was thought better to proceed for the present as they were proceeding. One was that it was possible legisla- tion would be Introduced on the recommendation of the joint committees of both Houses on municipal trading TV other reason was that in Warrington they had been fortunate in connection with their accounts, as it had been the invariable rule for a chartered or incorporated accountant to audit the accounts, although they might have been appointed as elective auditors and assisted by the Mayor's auditor. The audit had been full and real, and it was not quite economical to go to the expense of having the accounts audited twice over by a professional man. He repeated the assertion that they had nothing whatever to conceal.
The minutes were passed. WATER UNDERTAKING.
THE FINANCIAL POSITION.

The Borough Treasurer submitted to the Water Com- mittee the balance-sheet of the water undertaking for the year ended 31st March last, showing a deficiency of £1,299 14s. 4d., which had been made up out. of accumu- lated profits. Alderman EVA:CS and Councillor DUNCAN having pro- posed and seconded the acoption of the Water Com- mittee minutes,

Alderman BENNETT said he thought this statement was exceedingly misleading. Tt was the old question which the opponents of municipal trading continually trotted out. They tried to make out that no profit had been made unless it was a profit over and above payment of sinking fund and interest. Every business man knew that that was an entirely unfair way of representing the position. He (Alderman Bennett) would like to know what was the actual gross trading profit made by the Corporation on the water undertaking during the year. He understood it was a big amoßnt. Councillor HAWTHORN said the Borough Treasurer might tell them what the accumulated profits were. The BOROUGH TRF:ASURER said the gross profit for the year amounted to £16,305. (Hear, hear.) Then they had to pay sinking fund mud interest charges amounting to £17,605. Alderman BENNETT observed that probably a public company would have paid a dividend. There was really no deficiency, but a very handsome profit. _ _

Councilloil'EmmarroN said he iliffered with Alder- man Bennett. The Corporation had not got the capital like a private trading firm. They borrowed the money to build the works. They had to pay interest on that money, which was a profit charge. Before they got at really the net profit they were entitled to deduct that. Mr. Fairhurst's figures of £17,605 were not correct. The only deduction they were entitled to make was sinking fund and not the interest. Aldermen BENNETT said he did not agree with Coun- cillor Pemberton.

In answer to a question by Dr. Joseph as to whether, a§ time went on, the repayments would become less. The CHAIRMAN replied, "Oh, c3rtainly. In 35 years, I suppose. we shall pay it off." Councillor Dr. JOS'EPH : If they there is a deficiency of ,£1,209 now, that may he converted into a surplus ? The CHAIRMAN: Quite's°. We are gradually pay- ing off. Councillor WILKINSON said the differonce between tin Corporation and a limited liability company N-as that the capital of the latter was subscribed in shares. A company did not pay off year by year a certain amount of money to a sinking fund, so that at the end of 35 years it had bought itself out. The Corporat;on paid off the capital borrowed and redeemed an under- taking in a number of years for the good of the people of Warrington.

Councill7ir BALL said he believed some members of the Council continually misrepresented the parallel between a municipal undertaking and a limited com- pany. The water undertaking was supposed to have shown a loss of something like £1,400, and it was said that only the sinking fund should be allowed when they were trying to arrive at the net profits. The interest on the capital charge was not in this instance just the same as dividends paid to shareholders. In the case of a shareholder they did not pay interest on capital, hut, dividends. In arriving at the net profits they did sot reckon the dividends. He (Councillor Ball) asserted that the information rendered by Alderman Bennett was quite in order and that they were entitled to consider the interest and sinking fund as part of the protlts of the undertaking. The minutes were approved.
