Stringer, her carter,was similarly summoned.—Mr. Timrnis,Tnspector of Weights and Measures, said the carter had been sum- moned because Mrs. Broadhurst described him as her manager, and it would be for the magistrates to decide who was responsible. He (Mr. Timmis) saw the cart in Egerton-street on the morning of May 14th. There were nine bags, seven supposed to he cwt. bags, and two half cwt. bags. There were no labels on the bags. He asked Stringer to weigh the small bags. He did so. One was 561 b. and the other 541 b. He then asked him to weigh the large bags, and he said he had only one: 561 b. weight. He told him to take the cart to the yard, and the bags were then weigher] in the presence of Mrs. Broadbent. .One was the right weight, and the six others were 101, 109, 101, 104, 102, and 10Slbs. Broadhurst told Stringer that that came of him guess- ing the weights.—Mrs. Broadhurst now said that she had been ill and was totally ignorant of what had occurred.—Stringer said he left one of the weights hr : the yard and when be got to the station he guessed the weights, intending to check them at the yard. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.

The comments of the Tariff A COLD Reform newspapers on the DOUCHE. report of the Imperial Con- ference have great interest and significance. They show for one thing how easy it is to drift away from the most ordinary commonsense under the influence of a political prepossession. They show much more than that. They evince a determined disposition to persevere with the misrepresentations that are refuted by the report. One leading Tariff Reform newspaper, to take a single example out of many, has the effrontery to maintain that the version of what is now called "the Yellow Press" ought to be preferred to the report issued by the King's Printers. One of the most important uses of the Conference," it says "was definitely frustrated when the daily record of its proceedings was entrusted to the amateur instead of the professional journalist." The insinuation is that the Government frustrated the intentions of the Conference in the manner thus referred to. But it has been stated again and again in the House of Commons that the Govern- ment had nothing to do with the reports daily issued to the Press. The form and extent of these were matters determined by the Conference itself.

Indeed, the question of amateur and professional journalism does not enter into the case at all. It might have been advisable to throw the Confer- ence open to the public, and, therefore, to the whole of the Press. On that subject we say nothing, except that what was done at the last Conference precisely followed the lines of what was done at all previous Conferences. The Govern- ment, having nothing to conceal, did not interfere in any way with the proceedings, except by taking part in them, as the previous Government had done. Reports of proceadin,gs of this nature, it may be pointed out, are never the I work of professional journalists in their capacity as professional journalists. They are the work of professional shorthand writers. In this every accuracy is secured, A summary may be admirable from many points of view. It may be brilliant, or entertaining, or caustic, or merely humorous, but where affairs affecting the Empire are concerned, it is better that we should have the ipsissima verba, which is what we get through the shorthand report. The reporting has, in fact, been excellent. We obtain a record of all that was ' actually said, without bias or prejudice of any kind. Beyond that what is it possible reasonably to desire?
It is easy, of course, to understand why th Yellow Press should be dissatisfied with a verbatim report, and should express its preference for work done by professional journalists. The

verbatim report absolutely destroys the whole of its fictions. Sir ROBERT BOND did not make the scene attributed to him. He said none of the things that were reported. Mr. DEAKIN explained into entire reasonableness his phrase about the "cold shoulder." The report proves conclusively that not one of the stories by means of which the Yellow Press endeavoured to prejudice the mind of the country, and at the same time to maka mis- chief between ourselves and our Colonies, had any foundation in fact. Besides which, it exhibits the entire vagueness, and, we are sorry to say, the entire selfishness of the Colonial notions as to Preference. We are far from surprised, therefore, that the Tariff Reform Press should dislike a verbatim report. We admit that such a report in such quarters must be entirely disagreeable.

The Warrington Bridge WARRINGTON scheme has hung fire for a BRIDGE. very long time, and nothing has yet been done though plans have come to a head more than once. It seems ages since widening by cantilevers was decided upon after a long struggle against a pre- judiced opposition. The contract for the workwas even let to a local builder, bdt the bridge never budged and is still no wider. Then another scheme took shape—for a new bridge on a more modern or less expensive principle than stone and cement, but Ibis had also been lost sight of until questions at Tuesday's Council meeting elicited the fact that the scheme was nearly complete and would be pre- sented to the Council at an early date. From what we can learn the proposal is to construct an entirely new bridge on the ferro-concrete principle —the bridge to be one of a single span and 60 feet wide. If the new scheme makes no better pro- gress than the old some of us will never see the successor to the narrow stone bridge which has conveyed and congested the traffic of two counties for so many generations.

Councillor Stott carried his DEPUTATIONS OR motion to obtaie a return of PICNICS. all Corporation deputation expenses during the last three years, by twelve votes to ten at Tuesday's Council meeting. The motion created a record in its way, for we never before recollect a special resolution being carried without a single support- ing or dissentient speech other than that of the mover. Possibly, something was due to Coun- cillor Stott's eloquence, but appsrently those who did not desire a return of their deputation ex- penses were averse to rising and publicly voicing their objections. Ten of them stood up to vote, however, and it was remarked that in the main they were the gentlemen who of tenest served on deputations, The mover of the resolution framed his speech in temperate lanaguage and refrained from making any extravagant charges. But he pointed out that a stay in London of seven days by the Mayor cost £l7, while the attendance of the Mayor and Town Clerk at the annual meeting of the As.ociation of Municipal Corporatious cost £2O and there was no report by either as to the business of the meeting. In reckoning up the cost of another visit by the Town Clerk to London, Councillor Stott added the proportion of the official's salary for the time being to the expense. The total came to £37—which he said was more than hundreds of families in Warrington had to live upon during the past ten months. This was the poorest illustration and the weakest argument Councillor Stott used, and had really " nothing to do with the case." We see no objection to fairly generous expenses being allowed by a Corporation to those members who are willing to give their time and trouble on a deputation. If they will do the work without fee or reward of any kind so much the more to their credit, bet they should not be blamed if they expect reasonable " expenses." Whether those allowances in the past have been reasonable we shall know when the report is pre- sented. Councillor Stott's inquisitiveness can do no harm, and we commend his contention that there should be a report from deputations to annual meetings and conventions. There is too frequently no apparent return for the expenditure involved.

The publican has fallen on THE PUBLICAN'S evil days, judging from LAMENT. information which was given to the Warrington Assess- ment Committee yesterday. An appeal was made for the reduction of the assessment of a country hotel and in supporting it Mr. Collins, of London, an experienced valuer,offered some striking observa- tions which should give a little encouragement to temperance reformers. During the past few years, he said, he had valued over 5, 000 licensed houses and wherever he went he found that trade had gone down enormously. As an illustration he quoted a newspaper ataement that in the booths at Epsom on Derby Day,the sale of non-i ntoxicants was exceedingly large as compared with alcoholic liquors. Mr. Collins put down the general reduc- tion in the sale of drink to a great extent to education. Certainly greater prominence has been given in the schools of late years to illustrating the harmful effects of alcohol, while improved general education has no doubt done much to teach men the true interests in life. If Mr Collins' conclusions are correct—and happily there is reason to believe that they are—we cannot feel sorry for "the trade," but only hope that the people of England are realizing more clearly the folly of intemperance and are making progress, however slowly, along the pathway of sobriety.

Cfne of the most serious THE CHURCHES problems confronting the AND THE MASSRS. Churches of to-day is how to reach the great number of the people who seldom, if ever, are seen within the precincts of a place or worship. As the masses will not go to church the Free Church Council of Warrington is adopting a logical attitude and is going to the masses and,on Sunday a series of open air services was successfully launched. The site selected for the opening of the campaign was an admirable one. In the centre of the town, in Corporation-street, the constant stred.ms of people flowing along the main street, were diverted and an inspiring scene was presented by the assembling of a large and much mixed crowd. "Corner boys " ,nd idlers whose faces were stamped with the indelible imprint of utter helplessness, or bore evidence of their wasted lives, impelled by a passing curiosity stopped to join the throng; the frivolous youth of the town had their, interest aroused and many ceased their purposeless parade of the main thoroughfare to swell the ranks and hear with interest the vigorous aod practical addresses which were delivered by the Revs. J. F. Matthews and C. L. Stowe, and altogether the crowd was composed largely of those whom it was desired to reach. Popular hymns were sung with the greatest enthusiasm and everything seemed to point to much good being done by the services. May such be the lull and ample reward of the promoters and may their efforts lead to a quicken- ing of the religious life of the town I

The United Kingdom does not stand alone in the extraordinary prosperity shown in her trade returns. The United States of America last year had a remarkable period of commercial activity. The crops during 1906 were enormous. Wheat, it is true, did not break the record of 1901, but it yielded no less than 735,000,000 bushels. Maize beat that hollow, however, with 2,927,000,000 bushels; and the total of the five leading cereal crops—wheat, maize, oats, barley and rye—reached the unprecedented figure of 4,839,873,000 bushels, representing a value of £1,360,000,000 sterling! In the face of figures like these the inhabirants of smaller and older countries may well stand amaz•id. And all this prosperity took place in conditions not exceptionally propitious. Labour wit; short, in spite of the fact that the inflow of iannigranta totalled over 1,000,000 people during the year. The railways were quite unable to cope with the demamds made upon them for the transport o
AMERICAN PROSPERITY.

div.p: The art or science of flying is making such rapid progress that the opinion was becoming general locally that the Corporation was purposely delaying the Warrington Bridge improvement until the victory over the air was complete. Flying machines would do away with a lot of road and bridge-making, and might even solve the problem of the dust nuisance. " The splendid victory of liessrs. Crosfield's band at New Brighton has given great satisfaction locally, and it was pleasing to see what a large number of towns- people assembled to hear the performance in the park on Thursday evening. The cup which the band secured in competition with some of the best musical organizations or the North, occupied a prominent place in the stand, and the programme included "II Trovatore "—the New Brighton test pieoe. The playing in this as in each of the other selections was brilliant, and what particularly impressed one was the rapt attention with which the crowd listened. They gathered round the bandstand and followed every piece with manifest pleasure, not infrequently applauding. Special praise is due to Mr. Bedforth who conducted.

There is much satisfaction in local commercial circles at the second victory over the Ship Canal Company which the Warrington Corporation and Traders have gained this week. They have succeeded in their efforts to get a protective clause inserted in the Ship Canal (Various Powers) Bill which empowers the Company to pump from the estuary into the upper reaches of the Canal. IWarringtm's fear has been that the saltness of the river water might thus be increased, and the clause granted by the Commons Committee entitles them to compensation for any harm which they can prove to be due to increased salinity of the water flowing over Woolston Weir as the resat of the pumping opera- tions. The victory is a considerable one, and the clause cl valuable asset, but we do not suppose it will prevent future litigation on the point. Tne Canal Company will pump as much as they like, and proof of damage for which they are responsible will not be easily proved by the Corporation and traders. Still, the clause must have its restraining influence on the Company, who are bound to exercise caution in the matter.

Coming Events. The thirty-seventh annual meeting of the Warring- ton Workingmen's Permanent Benefit Building Society will be held in the Golborne-street schools on Monday evening. The quarterly meeting of the Warrington and Dis- trict Tradesmen's Association will be held in Toft's Assembly Room, Bridge-street, on Tuesday evening. A special service will be held at St. Barn abas' Church on Tuesday evening in celebration of the patronal festival. The Rev. Canon Matthew,Rector of Wigan, will preach. The Corporation of Warrington to stand over for a week. The Ship Canal Company are asking for an interim injunction to prevent the Corporation interfering with their taking control of the sluices at Walton. Taxation of Land Values. The third excursion of the Warrington Branch of the E.L.T.L.V. was made on Saturday last to Frodsham Hilt. In spite of the threatening weather in the early afternoon there was a good attendance. Mr. Fox, of Liverpool, read a number of splendid poems of Miss Torkington's, all dealing with the great fundamental injustice for the abolition of which this league is fighting. A house to house distribution of literature by the members in some parts of Frodsham ended a very pleasant excursion. On Saturday, June 22nd at 3.30 p.m. a great demonstration in favour of the Taxation of Land Values will be held at Belle Vue Gardens, Manchester. NORFOLK SUITS from 18/6—Bamcs,Outfitter.—Aclvt. The officiating priest was the Rev. Father Roche, and the ceremony was witnessed by a large congregation. The bride wore a becoming dress of cream voile and a white crinoline bat to match and was attended by NlissNora Maria Eckersley who wore a delaine dress'and hat to match. Mr. Percy C. He thought a great improvement would be made by the appointment of a resident inspector and, personally, was in favour of contributing tovri.tr.dt his salary.

MATHiit said he under-alood that there was already a resident inspector, and he did not see how a contribution by the Council towards his salary was going to make him more keen to stop the smells. It was decided to adjourn the question for a month to enable the Clerk to make enquiries.
NEW SCHOOL.

The St. Helens Education Authority have quite a number of new schools in course of construction, besides extensions to the Cowley Middle Schools. The latest school to be decided on is the new Cowley Council school, for which the Local Government Board have sanctioned the borrowing of £13,52G. The Com- mittee have adopted the new regulations of the Board of Education with respect to the preliminary education of elementary school teachers, and the Cowley Governors, who have charge of the education of scholar- ship students, have decided to appoint as bursars boys or girls who intend to become in the future elementary school teachers and are attending full time at the • Cowley Schools, as it is more advantageous than train- ling pupil teachers under the existing system.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.
Spittle Bridge Improvement-
COUNTY COUNCIL APPROVE THE
SMALLER SCHEME.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bevvsey Chambers on Wednes- day. Dr. Murray presided and there were present : Messrs. R. Forshaw, G.Mather, W. Stanier,J.Backhouse, J. Brooks, W. Houghton, W. Furness, J.C.Sutton (clerk), F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer). _

IIZAVY MOTOR TRAFFIC. In reference to a complaint made at the previous meeting with reference to heavy motor traffic on the roads the CLERK said he had received s letter from the Clerk to the Lancashire County Council in which he pointed out that" the weight of a heavy motor waggon unloaded is limited by the Heavy Motor Car Order to not exceeding five tons and a loaded one to not exceed- ing 12 tons. By the Highways and Locomotive Act 1878 the weight of a traction engine must not exceed 14 tons except the special permission of the County Council be obtained and such permission is only given by the County Council for the use of such an engine for the haulage of large single articles which could not be hauled by an engine less than 14 tons in weight. You will thus see that the County Council have no authority to limit the use of traction engines except those which exceed 14 tons."
SPITTLE BRIDGE IMPROVEMENT.
COUNTY COUNCIL APPROVE THE SMALLER SCHEME

The CLERK reported the receipt of the following letter from Mr. Crompton Hall, County Bridge Master: I was instructed by the Main Roads and Bridges Com- mittee to inform you that they regret that the heavy expenditure involved by the diversion scheme which your Council support is not in their opinion justified by the circumstances of the case; and they must adhere to their resolution approving of the smaller scheme, included in which of course are the three smaller road widenings, estimated to cost £1,053 3s. 10d. exclusive of land.l still hope that your Council will consider this the most adequate scheme that can be effected at reasonable cost, and I have to ask them through you to acquire the land necessary for 'carrying it out. Immediately you advise me that this has been done I shall be in a position to commence the work. Mr. MA.THER gave notice that at the next meeting of the Council he would move the adoption of the smaller scheme.

div.head: SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT AT SANKEY.
div.p: SUGGESTED IMPROVEMENT AT SANKEY.

Mr. Fumes* wrote :—As suggested by the District Council.on Thursday I had an interview with Mr. James Knowles of the Great Sankey Post Office, with refer- ence to the small plot of land at the corner of Chapel- road and Liverpool-road of which he is the owner with the object of trying to induce him to give it to the Council for the purpose of improving the approach to Chapel-lane. This he declines to do but will consent to sell his right for £3 and set back his fence as required. This will make a very desirable improvement and I would suggest that you or Mr. Newcombe take up the matter with the object of securing better terms ,but in any case to acquire the land. Mr. NEWC-OMBE in reply to a question said the price asked for the land was about £1 per yard. _ _ _
The matter was left in the hands Of Mr. Newcombe and the Improvement Committee.
ALKALI MANUFACTURE.
RESIDENT INSPECTOR FOR RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

Mr. C. L. Eva,Ns, agent to Sir Richard Brooke, wrote enclosing a copy of a letter from Messrs. Gibbons and Arkle (Liverpool), and expressing the hope that the council would see their way to contribute £ll 14s. 7d. as suggested. Messrs. GIBBONS and Arkle pointed out that shortly after the passing of the Act of 1882 arrangements were made with the Local Government Board wloreby there was to be a resident inspector for the Widnes and Run- corn area, one half of his salary being discharged by the Local Government Board and the other half by the City of Diverpool and five outside authorities according to rateable value. Liverpool had declined to continue the arrangement except upon a revised footing. The half salary amounted to £231 Bs. ld. per annum,and there was still left to be provided .221 14s. id., and it was suggested that the Rnncorn Rural District Council should pay £lO, and the Warrington Council £ll 14s. Bd. It was thought that this would enable them to bring greater pressure to bear upon the Inspector and also upon the manufacturers to ensure the manufacture being carried on with as little damsge to the neighbour- ing county as possible. Mr. 24EWCOMBE said only one estate was affected in their district, and it seemed like practically asking for a grant for the protection of Sir Richard Brooke's estate.

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

Widespread regret was occasioned at St. Helens on , Tuesday night by the death of Dr. Thomas Mulholland Bellew, of Victoria-square, which occurred after a long and painful illness. Dr. Bellew was a native of Strinagh, near Drogheda, but he had been in practice at St. Helens for the past twenty-five years, during which time he had been most popular. He was surgeon for the Lowe House Men's Guild, Holy Cross Boys' Guild, the Great Central Railway, and two of the local copper and smelting works. Over a year ago he was attacked by a serious malady, for which, since October last, three operations had been performed. Since Friday last he had been in a semi-conscious state, and died peacefully on Tuesday night shortly after eight o'clock at the age of fifty-three, his birthday falling the day before he died. He leaves a widow and five children, with whom the greatest sympathy is expressed. ST. HELENS FIRE BBTGADE AND AMBULANCE IMPROVEMENTS. At Newton Sessions last Thursday,'Mr. C. H. Unsworth applied on behalf of Alice Budworth, of Sheffield Row, Vulcan, for protection against her husband Charles Budworth. He said the man was a blacksmith at Vulcan Foundry, only about 24 years old, while the wife was only about 21, and they had been married less than six months. Short as that period was, the man had behaved as such a perfect brute that the woman had no alternative but to come to the Bench. She was confined in April, and only three days after that he assaulted her and followed that up by striking the baby in the face when it was a fortnight old. On Friday, at 11.30, he went home, and in consequence of his violence she had to go out, and he locked her out all night.' Those were some of the acts of a man whose actions seemed to be unaccountable except on the score of such an unnaturally brutal temper that no woman could live with him.- -Complainant gave evidence bearing out this state- ment.-Mr. Knowles submitted to Mrs. Badworth that she was jealous of a young woman named Maggie Crane and a Mrs. Garrity, and her husband was jealous of a young man named Teddy Clark, and that though he admitted having struck her, she had attacked him with a poker.-Plaintiff said she was not jealous, and when she hit him with the poker he deserved it, for he hit ther with the baby in her arms. If she had had more strength she would have given him more.-Mr. Knowles: Of course, he is a blacksmith and used to iron. Further evidence having been given Mr. Knowles said the defendant had begged his wife return to him. They had married while young and in a hurry, and both ot them were hot-tempered. If she had summoned him for assault and he had been bound over to keep the peace, they would probably have lived comfortably afterwards. It was an unfortunate case if either side should win it. Without calling witnesses to prove that it was the young woman's fault,he would ask the Bench to adjourn the case for a month in the hope that the Police Court Missionary might make peace between the parties and bring them together again.-The Chairman thought that would be a good thing, and especially if they could get a house in another neighbourhood. -The case was, however proceeded with, but after hearing more evidence the Chairman said there was not sufficient evidence for a conviction. The Bench hoped the Police Court Missionary would be able to bring the parties to a reconciliation. The summons would be dismissed.-The Police Court Missionary said he would do his best.
DROWNED IN THE SHIP CANAL.

On Saturday evening the Ship Canal at Runcorn was the scene of a sad drowning accident and a gallant attempt at rescue. A boy named Edwin Green. aged eleven years. son of Mr. John Green, of Blantyre-street, was sitting on the "ferry slip," when, by some means,he over-balanced himself and fell into the canal. He could swim a little, and he struck out and managed to reach the piles of the Transporter Bridge, but he could not get a hold, and sank. A youth of sixteen, John Lister, of Greek-street, saw the occurrence, and he divested him- self of his coat and plunged into the water. He reached the piles just as Green rose again, but missed grasping him by a few inches, and the unfortunate boy sank to rise no more. An hour later the body was recovered by Mr. Bylield, of the Grappling Corps. At the inquest, held on Monday, a verdict of" Accidentally drowned was returned, and Lister's brave conduct was praised.

The currant-loaf remains moist much longer than the plain one, and Currant Bread that is a day old is perfect for cutting. It, is necessary that the fruit should be cut through in order that its full flavour should be enjoyed. That is why, in the case of this most wholesome and nutritious bread, children, as well as adults, should be allowed the luxury of thin slices. Military Funeral. The remains of the late Private T. Tryner, of C Company of the Ist Volunteer Battalion P.W.V. South Lancashire Regiment, whose death took place last week, were interred at the Cemetery on Sunday with full military honours. The band, firing party, and lank and file to the number of about 120 attended under the command of Major Appleton. Deceased had been in the company since November Ist, 1902, and was Ihighly popular. At the conclusion of an impressive service volleys were fired over the grave and the "Last Post" was sounded.

A ST. lIBLENS BOY KLEPTOMANIAC.

Samuel Pigot, aged 12 years, of Harris-street, was charged at St. Helens on Saturday with stealing two pigeons. He belonged to a respectable family, but was out of the control of his mother, who was a widow. This was the fifth offence.—He was committed to an industrial school.

div.head: CYCLISTS AT RAINFORD CHURCEL
div.p: CYCLISTS AT RAINFORD CHURCEL

The third annual cyclists' service arranged by the St. Helens and Ormskirk clubs was held on Sunday at Rain- ford Church. Notwithstanding the stormy weather, there was a congregation of nearly four hundred, the cyclists representing the St. Helens C.C., St. Helens Recs.,Ormskirk, Skelmersdale, Rainford, St. Thomas's (St. Helens), Sutton Parish, and Parr. Canon Bridger preached on the "Liberty of the Gospel." He rejoiced to see so many cyclists there. On behalf of his colleagues and the officers of the church he gave them a hearty welcome, because by their presence there they showed that they acknowledged God, they signified that they believed that, with all their exercise and with all they were doing on the Sunday,God required something from them,and-they were there that afternoon giving it. He knew, and no doubt it was the experience of all of them, that those Sundays were the happiest, the purest, 1 the most rich in blessing in which the spiritual part of 1 man was attended to. The collection for the Bell- ringers' Fund realised £4. Mr. W. R. Graham presided at:the organ.

div.head: 'ELECTRIC LIGHT REDUCED.
div.p: 'ELECTRIC LIGHT REDUCED.

The St. Helens Electricity Committee have during the past week discontinued the use of arc lamps for street lighting, and substituted along all the main streets high-power incandescent lamps on the electric trolley poles. The committee has reduced the price of electricity charged to the St. Helens Post Office, the St. Helens Hospital, and the Borough Sanatorium from to 341 per unit. The Town Clerk has been instructed to obtain full particulars of the new by-laws and regula- tions which the Tramway Company have proposed. The Board of Trade have appointed Lieutenant-Colonel Von Donop to inspect the tramways and report. The committee propose to increase the salary of Mx. Hollingsworth, the electrical engineer, from £4OO to £425 per annum.

"A PRACTICAL (?) REFORMER." Sir,—l note that some contributor, who conceals his identity under the above ambiguous nom-de-plume, has been taking me to task in reference to my remarks anent the municipalization of the drink traffic. Now I take it, a practical as distinguished from a common or garden reformer, is one whose suggestions have been applied to the touchstone of .experience ; one whose theories are detail perfect and .hall-marked in every link; one who lacks the imagination to build up the ideal from the real ; and one who would require that every reform should be proved efficacious before it was given a trial. Obviously, no reform can be proved to be practical until it has been given a trial. Therefore, the man who rails at new suggestions of reform, because they are not practieal, is about as wise as the mother who forbade her children to go near the water until they could swim.

"Practical Reformer," however, demonstrates how little he is entitled to use the first part of his nom-de-plume by his ridiculous and illogical remarks, for, "as a practical alternative to my erroneous quack

div.head: SWIMMING.
div.p: SWIMMING.

There was a good attendance at the Baths, Legh- street, on Thursday evening last to witness the opening of the swimming season. The events were a 30 yards junior members' handicap and a Liverpool and District water polo match, Warrington v. Southport. For the junior race there were 17 entries, and some very good swimming was witnessed. S. Roberts secured the Ist prize, A. Warburton 2nd prize, H. Beaman 3rd. Unfortunately the Southport team missed their con- nection at Wigan and did not arrive until 9.30. In the interval there was a squadron race and a junior polo match. The result of the Southport match was a victory for the local team by 5 goals to 1. The scorers for the winners were C. Ashton 3, C. Turner and %V. Ashton. During the evening R. Allen,a club member, swam SOO yards for the purpose of obtaining one of the swimming club certificates,his time being 4 min. 19 sec. The next league match is with Everton away on June 12th. raehe committee have arranged a Polo match between St. Helens Juniors and Warrington Juniors. The away match will be played at St. Helens on July 4th, this being the occasion of the St. Helens v. Brussells match, and should prove very interesting. . . . .

The varidits works 'secretaries iire reminded that the entries for the works squadron competition close on Monday next, June 10th. It is to be hoped that as manY teams as possible will be represented and so make it a great success.

div.head: --- Savage Assaults at Warrington.
div.p: --- Savage Assaults at Warrington.

A fierce struggle between constables and prisoners was described at the Warrington Police Court on Saturday when John Ward, Dakin's-yard, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Church-street at 20 minutes past two on Fridsy afternoon, and also with assaulting P.C. dough; Patrick Ward, Dakin's- yard,was charged with having'been drunk and disorderly at the same time and place, and with having assaulted P.C. Malpas; whilst Margaret Ward was charged with assaulting P.C. Clough and a young man named John Gallop. P.C. Clough stated that he was on the Cemetery car going home at 20 minutes past two on Friday afternoon when he saw the three prisoners, along with another woman, creating a disturbance at the end of Mersey- street. The two men were drunk and the women were under the influence of, drink. They had been put off the car for using obscene language. Witness got off the car and told them about twenty times to go home and behave themselves. They would not go and he proceeded to take them into custody, whereupon they became very violent. He was struggling with John Ward, and was lip And down on the ground with him for ten minutes. Ward said, "he would serve him (witness) liked he served a policeman 16 years ago." Margaret Ward took her clog off and struck witness on the head with it whilst he was on the ground. P.C. Malpas came up and took hold of Patrick Ward. Witness's whistle was thrown away so that it could not be used. Be would have been very roughly handled if his wife had not interfered. P.C.'s Holland and Redding- ton came on the scene, and with the assistance of two young men they took prisoners into custody. The officers were knocked and kicked about like a football. Prisoners were "more like lions than anything else." Witness was struck in the face, and his mouth bled. He had a very severe struggle. Evidence Of the assaults was given by P.C.'s Malpas and Reddingtonand John Gallop and Arthur Brown who pluckily assisted the officers. Superintendent Monaghan said that was John Ward's 14th appearance. He had been up three times for assaul- ing the police, and once for wounding the police, for which he was sent to gaol for 12 months, and that officer who was injured suffered from his bruises up to the day he died. Patrick Ward was his brother, and be had been convicted five times for assaulting the police. They were terrors to policemen. The woman had not been summoned before. He pressed the case against the men as they were very dangerous. John and Patrick Ward were eash sent to gaol for three months with bard labour, and Margaret Ward was lined 10s. and costs (21 Gs.), or 14 days' imprisonment in default.
The Bench complimented Brown and Gallop for assisting the police, and they were also thanked by Superintendent Sionaghan. Each was given 2s. 6d. as a reward.

div.head: ANOTHER WOMAN ARRESTED.
div.p: ANOTHER WOMAN ARRESTED.

Elizabeth Ellen Ward pleaded guilty, at the Warring- -bin Police Court, on Tuesday, to assaulting Police- constable Malpas, last week,in Church-street. Prisoner was concerned in the street scene which occurred on Friday afternoon, and when the officer, who was in plain clothes, went to the assistance of Police-constable Clough, who was getting roughly handled by three of the prisoner's relations' she kicked him on the legs and struck him several timits in the face. Prisoner stated that she did not know that Malpas was a police officer. A fine of 10s. and costs (1 2s. 6d.) or fourteen days was imposed.

A statistician announces that "in 1904 the "United States produced 99 per cent. of the entire world's known production of natural gas." In that year, it will be remembered, we had both a long session of Congress and a Presiden- tial campaign.

An Easterner was prospecting in the north Georgia mountains, when he came on a native apparently clinging to the side of a steep hill, tilling corn. The prospector stopped for a chat, and the mountaineer, nothing loath for a rest in the shade from his fatiguing toil, was agree- able. "Say, friend, how in the world do you get the corn down off that hillside after it is ready for harvest?" asked the stranger. "In jugs," was the larconic and probably truthful reply.

GARLAND, 51. to E 5, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Personal. The Rev. E. B. Carleton, eldest son of the Rev. E C. E. Carleton, has recently entered upon his duties as vicar of Kamsach, .Saskatchewan, Canada. In a letter Mr. Carleton reports his arrival at Kamsach, after a very interesting railway journey of three and half days, starting from Montreal. On his arrival at 9.30 p.m. on Saturday night, May 11th, he was " spotted " by a young man, who guessed he was the "new parson,' and kindly gave him a hand with his personal luggage, taking him to the hotel, where he found very comfortable quarters. The following day (Sunday) he was taken to see the church, which he describes as a charming little mission room. Other friends called at the hotel during the day, from w,hom he received a most cordial welcome. He says he is as fit as possible, and quite hopeful in his anticipation of the work that lies before him. BLOUSES, a grand selection from is. Hid.— BANKS, Outfitter, Horsemarket st.—Advt. Proposed Yorkshire and Lancashire Single Tax Excursion. The following letter appears in the current issue of "Land Values" : "It has been suggested to us that it would be a very good idea to arrange, if possible, this summer— say, for August Bank Holiday—a joint excursion to some handy seaside or other resort, so that the Lancashire an Yorkshire members of the League for the Taxation of Land Values, and friends , and sympathisers, may have an opportunity of getting to know each other and of conferring together as to the best means of promoting the cause-in this district. If those of your readers who fall in with the idea will kindly send their names and addresses, and sugges- tions as to place of meeting, etc., to one or the other of us, we shall be very glad to take the matter in hand, and see what can be done.—Yours faithfully, R. Ockel, 9 Walton New-road, Lower Walton, War- rington ; F. Skirrow, 2 Darley-street, Bradford. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—IINDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. CELLULAR SHIRTS from 2/6 —Bmixs,Outfitter.-Advt. ; Bricklayers' Picnic. The members of the Warrington branch of the Operative Bricklayers' Society on Saturday visited Chester in celebration of the attainment of their majority. Dinner was served at the Nag's Head, after which the party numbering 75, had a trip up the river to Eccleston, and on returning to the city they assembled at the Temperance Hall, George-street, to hear an address by Mr. Batcheler, general secretary of the society. Mr. James Astley, secretary of the Warrington branch, presided, and was supported by Mr. J. Livingstone (president of the branch), Mr. W. Bradbury, Mr. Higginson (secretary of the Chester branch), Councillor W. Carr, Mr. G. Dodd (president of the Chester branch). A. vote of thanks was accorded to the speaker, on the motion of Mr. Bradbury, seconded by Mr Higginson, and supported by Councillor Carr. The day's outing proved very enjoyable.

Whitehouse and Clarke reaped a rich harvest among the wickets and the Old Boys total was only 20.

Low scoring was the order in the match between Sankey Wire Mills 2nd and Rylands on Saturday. Batting first none of the Longshaw-lane men reached double figures and Rylands were set 34 to get to win. This however proved beyond them and they retired beaten by seven runs. At the present time the Wire Mills 2ndls indulging in a litile self glorification at the expense of the first eleven as, whilst the seniors have won only one of their matches the juniors have not yet been beaten.

The matter was referred to the valuer. A NEWTON WORKS CLOSED. Mr. Herbert Hatton (Messri. Robert Davies and Co.) appealed against the assessment of the works of Messrs. Gillespie and Mason, Newton Paper Mills, at £738 gross and £546 ratable. He stated that the works had been closed down and he made the appeal on behalf of the receivers for the debenture holders. The place was being used for office and warehouse purposes but absolutely no manufacturing, was carried on. All the workmen were discharged in December. The matter was referred to the valuer. Mr. Hatton said the works were shortly to be offered for sale by auction and he hoped for the sake of Newton a purchaser would be found and the mills would soon be in full work again.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

THE CONGO ATROCITIES.—At the monthly meeting of the Padgate Wesley Guild held in the Wesleyan School on Monday evening a paper was read by Mr. Bert Mason on Optimism and Pessimism." The Rev. W* Mellor presided over a large attendance. A discussion on current topics ensued, and the following resolution on the Congo atrocities was approved on the motion of Mr. E. England, seconded by Dr. Bennett: 'That this meeting representing 140 members, protests against the condition of abject and cruel slavery in which the native races of the Congo continue to be held by the governing authorities of the Congo State, and calls upon his Majesty's Government to decline to recognize any scheme of Belgium annexation of that state, which is npt based upon the total reversal of the existing I system with its attendant inhumanities." In referencel to the Peace Conference the following resolution was carried "That this meeting expresses the earnest hope 1 that at the approaching Hague Conference his Majesty's representatives will do their utmost to promote the following objects, viz. : (1) The removal by mediation of the international difficulties sfb int) lead to expensive naval and military armaments. (2) Thelirnitation and ultimate reduction of armamentr, (3) The compulsory delay of incipient hostilities."

Exciting scenes were witnessed in connection with a fire which broke out early on Wednesday morning at the Royal Oak Inn, Bridge-street. Shortly after four o'clook a cyclist (Thomas Edwards) was passing the premises when he noticed that the tap-room was in flames. He at once roused Mr. and Mrs. McClinton, who found that their way to the ground floor was cut off by the fire and had to escape from the building through a bedroom window. In doing this Mrs. McClinton fell on to the glass roof of the bar parlour and bruised herself, whilst in jumping from the window the maid damaged her ankle. In the meantime Mr. Edwards had informed the police and information was sent to the Fire Station. The police forced their way into the building and with the Assistance of several civilians, poured buckets of water on to the flames, and by the time Superin- tendent Turner. and the brigade arrived with the steam engine the fire had been extinguished. The damage is estimated at £2OO and is covered by STRONG MAN'S LONELY DEATH. insurance. div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

Warrington's hope in the Lancashire and Cheshire Competition rests upon the Bull's Head players and right well are they able to uphold the honour of the town. On Saturday they triumphed over Cheetham Temple though not by quite so large a margin as one vqouldhave hoped. But still they won and the victory ought to inspire them with a determination to succeed in the concluding rounds of the tournament. Cemetery players were not no fortunate and there is sorrowing in their camp. In the first place several of their leading players were absent whilst Chorlton won by only six points.

Tbe match was an exciting one, not one single-figure return being made and some first-class bowling was witnessed. Warrington had the misfortune to be behind almost the whole match but fought gamely and Chorlton were not sure of their progress into the third round until the last two players were off the green. The last game witnessed one of the best fights of the after- noon. Alex Shaw was leading W. Swanton 8-1, and 10-4 when the Cemetery man found his length and ran to 18. all and then home. Scott and J. Valentine also had a good game. They peeled at 14 and 16, and then from 19-18, Scott reached game with two woods hone.

The play in the Warrington Works Competition on Saturday was not of an exciting character in each case the matches being won with ease. Some good games were however witnessed. It looked an easy thing for A. Ellison who opened well against J. Lawton and from 6-0 ran to 8-3 and 10-5. Then Lawton got in a run of ten and secured the verdict. T. Jefferson and D. Stokes had a similar game. Jefferson who was 4-3 and then 10-3 losing by the odd point after peeling at 11, 12, 13 and 14.

Twenty-three ends were necessary in the game between S. Fletcher and T. Lawton and in the end one point only separated the players. Lawton set off with a run of four and Fletcher promptly followed suit. The next points were divided when Fletcher got going and ran to 9-6. Lawton next bad a turn and was 12-9 before Fletcher again scored, and then he looked as thougb he had lost the game as Fletcher went to the front 14-12. He, however, refused to recognize defeat and with three well played singles secured the verdict. Turning to the other extreme D. Higham in 10 ends beat D. Feeney 154, the first point in the game, singu- larly enough, being secured with ease by the loser.

Then reason held sway again, and she replied in clear, coal tones: "No, Albert, you may think you would, but you wouldn't. You couldn't you know. Hardly a square inch of the world could be purchased on a salary of twenty-five shillings a week."
Coster (irritable through lack of trade): "Buy a box o' cough lozenges—'an g yer !" By. stander : "I haven't got a cold." Coster: "Then fight me, an' buy some stuff for blftek eyes!"

"Sermon stealers," said a minister, "ought to be careful. They ought to read over several times the sermons that they steal before deliver- ing them. I knew a young man of twenty-one or twenty-two who preached a stolen sermon he had not read over, and in the most impressive part he found himself declaiming : My friends, when I first came amongst you more than forty years ago, these thin, white blocks were thick and brown, and this bent back,' etc. Another ser- mon-stealer, preaching in a village of about a hundred souls, said, before he could check him- self :—‘ In the teeming streets of this great Metropolis.'"

It was a rural cricket match, and in the inter- val between one batsman's dismissal and another's arrival the village blacksmith, who had been piling up a larr score, left the crease and ambled to the .pavilion for a drink. On sauntering back to the wicket he passed the minister. "John," said the latter, 'you- could have done without that, you know. Look at that stream," pointing to where a brook crossed the meadow. "You should be like---" "Yes, sir," interrupted John, hastily, "you're right; I'm just like that stream—can't run when I'm dry.'

Some people seem to have a very unenviable aptitude for expressing their thoughts in such a manner as to turn what would, perhaps, be a compliment into a seemingly direct insult. A working-lad applied on one occasion to a country clergyman for a letter of introduction to a duke, of whom he wished to seek aid. "But why don't you go in person and see his grace?" asked the clergyman. "Well, you see, sir," was the nervous answer, " I don't like to speak to a duke. He may be wouldn't listen to the likes of me. I can talk to you well enough, sir, for, you see, there's nothing of the gentleman about you."

"Well, -girls, Jack and I are to be married at last, and we are so happy." "Did you and Jack have some trouble in getting your father's consent?" "No; but papa and I had a lot of trouble in getting Jack's consent." "Extenuating cir- cumstances?" asked his honour. "How do you make them out?" "He is a collector for a piano firm, and he called to demand an instalment on the/piano just while my daughter was practising and I was trying to read -ch.. paper."

div.head: WILLIE'S NARROW ESCAPE.
div.p: WILLIE'S NARROW ESCAPE.

Willie lived with his father and mother in the country. It was summer time. and Mr. Eirdsey decided to take his wife and Willie to the sea- side for the. holidays. So about the middle of July they went to spend two months at Yar- mouth. Willie was ten years old, and was de- lighted .at the prospect of going to the seaside. They started early one Monday morning, and arrived at Yarmouth about 6 o'clock in the evening. Mr. Birdsey had thoughtfully engaged rooms, so all they had to do was to wend their way to the house, and rid themselves of their luggage. Willie was very anxious to go out on the sands, but both his father and mother were too tired to go out after their long day's journey, so he was obliged to content himself w,th stay- ing indoors for the rest of the evening. Every morning Willie and his fathcr went out, either on the sands or elze to lo.')k round the town. As a rule. all three sent the at:ernoon on the sands, occasionally going for short trips in a steamboat.

One afternoon, after they had been at Yan'aouth about a month, Mrs. Biidi.cy did not feel very well, so Mr. Birdsey was obliged to slop in with her, and Willie, to his great delight. Wa :3 allowed to go on the sands by himself, only he was to be sure to be home in.good time for tea, and not to get into mischief. Willie marched off to the sands feeling quite delighted mat he had got an afternoon to himself to do what he liked. First of all, he played with his spade and pail, and at making sand castes, etc. When he had got tired of this, he took a walk round to look at the different people, and watch the niggcrs, who were singing on the sands.

At last, he went. close to the edge of the sea. and, spying at -a little distance alon;:„7 the coast some big logs of timber, he said to himself, " Hurrah I now I'll have some fun." 110 IMMO- diately ran to the place where the timber was. and began playing about on it. After a little while, a F.•.reht big wate came dashing up to the shore. which took Willie unawares. an carried him off his feet. Immediately anoth-...r wave, which was going out to ma. came ol and took Willie with it. He knew how t 4 Swin well enough in fresh water, but now he WaS quite baffled, for as soon as he tried to swim, a wave would come along and toss him, first to (Ale place and then to another. until at last poor Willie gave up hopes of ever getting back to the shore.

Fortunately for him, a gentleman on shore at this moment noticed his peril, and dashed into. the waters after him. In a few minutes they were back again on shore, but Willie had been shaken up so much that it was a few 'moments before he could get, his, senses together again. The gentleman then asked Willie who he was. and where he was staying. and offered to see Willie home. Upon arriving home, the gentlenian gave Mr. and Mrs. Birdsey a short account of what had happened, and concluded oy saying that Willie would take no harm if he went to bed at once and stayed there till morning. He then. rose to go. and Mr. Birdsey thanked him very much, Trossing him to take a small reward for his services, but the gentleman would no; hear of any such thing, and took his departure. Willie was at once put to bed, and, as the gentleman said, was as light as possible the next morning. .But he never for;.:;ot biz little adventure, and after the holidays were over. when he went back to school, be g:lve Inll account of it to his boy oompnni,;ns. MARGARET MARV

A SOBER DOG AND A DRUNKEN MASTER.' One night a farmer was driving home in the dark. Whilst On his way a dog came barking in front of his horse. The horse was afraid, and would not go on. The farmer, not knowing what to do, got out of his cart, followed the dog a little .way. and there, to his surprise, saw the dog's master lying he.plessly drunk across the pathway. Oh, dear Uncle Ned, wouldn't it be nice to have a friend as faithful as this dog?

Dear Uncle Ned.—l am sending you some pieces of poetry, which I hope will succeed in winning a prize. NOW HE KNOWS. Pussy had a mind to see All the wide world held, But his curiosity Once was rudely quelled. For a soda syphon stood In his path' one day, How to ope it Pussy would Quickly know the way. Round and round he gravely went, • Took its bearings well, Then, when half an hour was spent, To his work he fell.

I was reading a well-known halfpenny paper the other morning, and I noticed a photograph of a phenomenon which was seen in London recently, and which even the oldest inhabitant failed to recognise. Eventually, it was discovered to be the sun. Really, it's such a while since I saw it, that it's quite possible that I shall forget its shape, • and on some future occasion, if I'm asked what shape it is, am afraid I shall be thinking of the schoolmaster's two snuff-boxes, and say, `.' Square en Sundays and round on week-days." Of course, I shall be laughed at, my dears, but my questioner will have to put my ignorance down to want. of prac- tice. Well, amidst all these dreary days, I have had some bright moments, and they hate been when the postman has brought my mail. How you would have screamed to have seen such a host of funny Pig Cards. Fat Pigs, Lean Pigs, Old Pigs, Young Pigs, are all here, together with many animals far removed from tile porcine breed. One card, my dear friends, depicted something originally intended for a Piggy- Wiggy, but it conies out something after the style of an Elephant, with a concertina back and a Kangaroo tail. I only wish you could see it, you would enjoy the fun. The prize for the best Pig goes to W. Elliott, and Consolation Prizes have been sent to six other competitors. Next week the Pig Card Prizes will be con- tinued. With best of good wishes, from
lIN'CLE RED,
WELCOME TO • May Keene, Julia ;•:.inythe, Hetty Bane, Jack Webb, Georgie Burnett, Reggie White.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a story. It is called,
PROUD RICHARD,

Once upon a time there lived a Queen, who had SIX sons and six daughters. The eldest son was very proud, because, when his mother died, he was going to have all the property which his mother now possessed. The Six daughters- were invited to a large party, and also the six sons. The Queen said that they should have her grnrd coach, and drive to the party. The eldest son did not like the thoughts ot going to the party with his other brothers and sisters, so he said, "I will not go with my brothers and sisters. because they are not good enough for me." So he made his mother give him another coach, so that he might ride by himself. The Queen promised him a coach; but she said if he had it he could not have her property when she died. The son —who was named Richard—said that he would rather have the coach than the property, so his mother said he could have it. When they came back from the party. they found that their mother was dead. Richard was very sorry, and so he. said, "I wish, I had gone with my other brothers and sisters," but, of course, it was no good then. When he saw his mother's will, he was very angry, because the " property was divided between his five brothers and six sisters. His brothers and sisters grew up to be wealthy men and women, but he was very poor, and had to earn his living by going about the streets begging. This is what .Richard had fpr being so proud. AMY GOMER.

div.head: RAIN.
div.p: THE RAIN.

A merchant was riding home .from market, and had behind him his knapsack. in which there was a large sum of money. It rained very heavily, and the • good man was soon wet through, which annoyed him very Much, and he grumbled at the weather being so bad while he was obliged to travel. His way led through a thick forest. As soon as he had entered it. he saw. to his diAma;• a robber, who aimed at him with his gun; He would have been killed on the spot, out the rain had made the powder so damp that the gun missed fire. The traveller put spurs to his horse, and escaped the danger. - As soon as he was in safety, he said to him- self, " How foolish I was to grumble at the bad weather, instead of bearing it patiently, as sent from God! If the sky had been bright and the air dry, I might at this moment have been lying dead, and my wife and children would have ex- pected me in vain. The rain of which I com- plained has saved both my life and my property. For the future, I will never forget what the! proverb says:— " ` Take from God's hand whate'er He will bestow; 'Tis. best for thee, although tit seems not so.'" M. GARI.L.
Dear Uncle \Ned,—Many thanks for the lovely prize you sent me. This time I am sending you a story, called,
IN SAFE CUSTODY.

"Granny," said little Johnny, as he counted a lot of nuts somebody had kiv en him. "can yer eat nuts ?" "No, dear," said the old lady, "I haven't got any teeth." "Well, then,'' said Johnny, emptying his nuts into Granny's lap, "I'll give you these to mind till I come back." BERTHA LISTER.

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
WATERPROOF PORCELAIN CEMENT.

Dissolve (1) 10 parts of mastic in 60 parts of anhydrous . (absolute) alcohol, (2) 20 parts of isinglass in 100 parts of water and 10 parts of grain spirit, (3) 5 parts of gum am- moniac in 25 parts of grain spirit. Thoroughly mix solutions 1 and 2, then add solution 3, and boil the whole down to 180 parts.

div.head: SEA, RAIN, AND RIVERS.
div.p: SEA, RAIN, AND RIVERS.

Dr. Richard Fritzsche has recalculated from recent data the amount , of rain an- nually falling upon the earth's surface. He finds that it is equivalent to a layer of water of the uniform depth, for the whole globe, of about 351 in. The amount falling on the land is equivalent to a uniform depth of 29iin. Considering only the. land which is drained by rivers ?Lowing into the - sea, Dr. Fritzsche calculates that only 30 per cent. is returned to the ocean, and ,that the rest is removed by evaporation.

div.head: CRACKED CASTINGS.
div.p: CRACKED CASTINGS.

The founder who uses aluminium has to contend with cracked castings. A slight crack at the surface, and the work is ruined. And often it happens that the cracks are not conspicuous until machining takes place. Most of the difficulties are caused by the use of aluminium alloys, which contain zinc. It is the zinc which causes the trouble. These mixtures shrink more than other aluminium alloys. The cracking u.sually takes place in certain patterns in which the casting cannot shrink. In consecylnce of this cracking the übe or aluminium aud copper alloyea-Is -re- commended. They are not so strong, but owing to their superiority in casting they average better results than aluminium zinc alloys.

div.head: SUBMARINE MOUNTAINS.
div.p: SUBMARINE MOUNTAINS.

Phenomena, like the upthrust of a new island in Behring Sea, and the tremendous earthquake shock, evidently originating in the ocean bottom, felt at Apia in December, 1906, give fresh interest to the results of the exploration of the Pacific's floor made by the United States steamer Nero in surveying a trans-Pacific cable route. East of the Island of Guam a submarine mountain range was discovered, some of whose peaks rise within 689 fathoms of the ocean's surface, whereas the valleys between them descend to a depth of 5,000 fathoms. Here was made the deepest sounding on record, 5,269 fathoms, only 66ft. less than six miles. This abyss is now called the `; Nero deep."

div.head: SPIDER'S WONDERFUL EYES.
div.p: A SPIDER'S WONDERFUL EYES.

The Attus family of spiders, abounding in Java, have, in addition to numerous smaller eyes, a pair of large ones, which writers have called "gig-lamp" eyes. A specimen of the spider, captured near Buitenzorg, exhibited 'a remarlable power of changing the colour of its "gig-lamps." When it was captured the eyes were dark-brown' -like the body. But suddenly they changed to bright grass- green. Soon afterwards they turned back again from green to brown, and this change of colour was repeated several times in suc- cession, apparently at the will of the creature. Whether it was an effort of the spider to inspire terror in its enemy or an effect of its own terror is uncertain. Another singular fact is that the colour of either one or both eyes could thus be changed.

div.head: GASOLINE AS EXPLOSIVE.
div.p: GASOLINE AS EXPLOSIVE.

A gasoline tank rarely explodes. It cannot, declares the Scientific American, unless it contains gasoline . vapour and air in explo- sive proportions, which latter condition is al- most never present. It does not explode be- cause it contains too little air or too much gasoline. Even if a tank of gasoline were to burst from heat applied to its exterior, the ccnfined heavy gas would not explode if in contact with flame or fire, but would bilrn in- stead. True, a tank of gasoline with no vent could do considerable damage were it to burst and throw burning oil and flaming gas about, but 1,000 gallons of gasoline in a ves- sel's bilges would not be so dangerous from explosion as a hundredth of that amount.. Tho larger quantity would burn rapidly, while the smaller would be sufficient, if mixed with the proper amount of air, to utterly demolish almost any boat.

div.head: WHAT MAKES THE SKY BLUE.
div.p: WHAT MAKES THE SKY BLUE.

It is the atmosphere that makes the sky look blue and the moon yellow. If we could ascend to an elevation of fifty miles above the earth's surface, says Rene Bache, we should see that the moon is a brilliatt white, while the sky would be black, with the stars shining as brightly in the daytime as at night. Furthermore, as a most picturesque feature of the spectacle, we should take notice that some of the stars are red, others blue, yet others violet, and still others green in colour. Of course, all of the stars (if we bar the planets of our own system) are burn- ing suns, and the hues they wear depend upon their temperature. The hottest stars are blue. Thus Vega, in the constellation Lyra, is a blue sun, hundreds of times as large as our own solar orb. We are journey- ing in its direction at the rate of millions of miles a-day., and at some future time it may gobble us. all up. For, after all, humiliating though the confession be, our sun is only a very small star—of the sixth magnitude, or thereabout—and of an importance in tile univtrse so slight as to be scarcely within the pale of respectability.

div.head: MODERNISED SUN-DIAL.
div.p: A MODERNISED SUN-DIAL.

It seems odd to read that the modern man of business in his week-end retreat, as well as the owner of a country estate, with his motor-cars, wants to know the time with greater certainty than clocks and watches can give it, and to find there recommended to start a sun-dial! Hundreds of modern reproductions of the various forms of old sun-dials have, says a writer in Engineering, been set up partly for use and partly for ornament, but their usefulness is materially reduced by the difficulty of setting such dials with sufficient accuracy, and by the cum- brous arithmetical figuring entailed before Greenwich time is found. The helio-chrono- meter overcomes these difficulties. A simple operation of levelling sets the instrument, which indicates Greenwich time with a direct simplicity only approached by a per. clock. The idea is that the helio-chronometer shall serve as a standard of reference for correcting clocks and watches at convenient intervals say, once or twice a - week and experience proves that when once the clocks and watches have had their regulators set in accordance with the helio-chronometer observations, their in- dications of time may be relied on for the few days which may elapse between the observations,

div.head: REPTILIAN GIZZARD STONES.
div.p: REPTILIAN GIZZARD STONES.

The fact that the marine plesiosaurian rop- tiled of the oolitic and cretaceous epochs was in the habit of swallowing pebbles and re- taining them in their stomachs for the ap- parent purpose of assisting digestion, has for some time been familiar to paleontologists. New discoveries in America indicate that the great dinosaurian reptiles, such as Bronto- saurus and Diplodocus, had a similar habit. The evidence rests on the discovery in two instances of small heaps of specially-polished quartzitic pebbles in association with the skeletons of these reptiles. The pebbles are for the most part bright - coloured jaspers, and bear a polish quite different from that of the ordinary wind-polished or river-worn pebbles found elsewhere in the same beds, so that they ars quite unmistakable. In the one instance about two dozen were found to- gether, but in the second case the number was smaller. Very curious, comments the Field, is the fact that each heap included a, certain number of very bright-coloured fos- siliferous jaspers, which are uncommon in the strata, and suggest that the dinosauri were in the habit of picking out stones of this particular type for swallowing. A fur- ther suggestion is that the stomachs of these nebble-swallowina rentiles were furnished with gizzards like those of birds, as it is otherwise somewhat difficult to see how ,the pebbles can have acted efficiently and have been permanently retained in the stomach.
