div.head: Motors and Children.
div.p: Motors and Children.

'Sir,—As a motorist who believes in considerate driving, but who in return expects consideration, from others, may I ask parents whose children use the trams for attending school to caution them to exercise greater care in crossing the roadways, and generally to look where they are going. Only this morning, driving in from Stockton Heath, when passing a Warrington bound tram-car which had stopped half-way down Wilderspool Causeway on the off-side, I narrowly escaped running over a small girl, who, without the slightest warning, rushed out across the front of the tram-car. My speed at the time was 12 miles an hour per gauge.—Yours faithfully, Warrington, June 3rd.
HOLMAN KINGDON.

div.head: NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION.
THE PLYMOUTH MEETINGS. Mr. T. Shaw's Slashing Attack on
the Lords.

div.head: COMMONS MUST BE MASTERS.
div.p: COMMONS MUST BE MASTERS.

The annual meetings of the National Liberal Federation opened on Thursday at Plymouth. A wet and boisterous morning gave way to a whole after- noon of welcome sunshine, and it was under these improved weather conditions that the delegates assembled at two o'clock in the spacious and hand- some Co-operative Hall, for the discussion of many important subjects at present engaging attention. The attendance was about 2,000 strong, including some 120 ladies, and, with the exception of the question of de admission of women to the executive committee, every subject brought forward received the enthusiastic and unanimous support of the meeting. The outstanding feature of the proceedings was the outspoken speech of the Lord Advocate for Scotland, whose clever and unsparing attack on the Lords " brought down the house" on several occasions. In the chair, of course, was Ifr. A. H. D. Acland, the president, who was strongly supported on the plat- form, the occupants of which included Sir Edward Evans (chairman of the general committee),Sir Robert Hudson (general secretary), and several members of Parliament and other prominent Liberals. The Commons must be Master.

THE TREATMENT FOR THE HOUSE OF LORDS. "There must be no scheme of strengthening the House of Lords. This is a question of mastering. In a few days the Government scheme will be divulged. In this conflict between the two Houses the House of Commons must be the master definitely and conclu- sively." There was loud and prolonged cheering when Mr. Shaw made this declaration in moving a resolution con- demning the action taken by the House of Lords in destroying and mutilating measures passed by the House of Commons, a resolution he described as "a declaration and appeal from a strong and resolute people through a strong and resolute party to a strong and resolute Government." (Cheers). Resoluteness was not to be turned into mockery at the behest of an unrepresentative and irresponsible body of men. (Cheers). Having referred to the state of parties at the general election end now—the Govern- ment majority had been decreased by one—Mr. Shaw proceeded to discuss the situation. The right of veto had been stretched to the point of usurpation. The House of Lords had asserted and maintained an anti-popular sovereignty which, in the judgment of the Government and of the nation, was inconsistent with the cause of freedom and self-govern- ment. (Cheers.) Do not let any man or any body of men or any newspaper or any trust of newspapers— (cheers)—do not let them think that the Liberal party is going to be intimidated by these ongoings, either by noblemen or by them. (Loud cheers.) It was the House of Lords that had brought this question definitely within the region of practical politics. (Renewed cheera.) No longer were Liberals going either out- wardly to crouch or inwardly to tremble on account of them. (Cheers.) "We are," he centinned, "in the region of politics and out of the region of superstition." (Loud cheers.) The House of Lords had never supported an unpopular Cause that was right or thwarted a popular cause that was wrong. (Cheers). After referring to the inability of the House of Lords to interfere with Sir William Harcourt's death duties bu?get and the granting of the • Constitution to the 'Transvaal, the right hon. gentleman said with regard to the latter that they knew what the Lords would have 'done; they would have given the Transvaal a combina- tion of the Milner Constitution, and he would say to Lord Milner that even in the decadence of his influence to thought it would have been well if, consulting his own dignity as well as the dignity of the party to which he belonged, he had no longer cited his theory of the " top dog " with odious and ill-timed and vulgar brutality—(cheers)—which, looking to the present-day deep convictions of this nation, was insulting to a people who had wakened now to the glories of racial equalities and peace. (Renewed cheers.) The day was near when the power of the Lords must be crippled definitely and conclusively curtailed with regard to any obstacle which they desired to interpose between tho people of this country and the land which bore them. (Cheers.) "We are here as Liberals," he continued. "to strengthen the hands of the Prime Minister. (Loud cheers.) His charter is our charter— that the land of this country must become less a pleasure house for the rich and more a treasure house for the nation." (Cheers.)

div.head: DIE IS CAST.
div.p: THE DIE IS CAST.

The die was now cast; the Lords had challenged them and would bring up all their forces dressed with all their orders. There must be no sch'eme of strengthen- ing the House of Lords. This was a question of master- ing. When in a few days the Government scheme was divulged, be sure that there would be no mistake, no beatingabout the bush about that. If Liberals were only true to themselves their forces were stronger far than those opposed to them, for they included the support of healthy national ambitions, the uplifting of a belief in the natural, a passioa for social progress,for even-handed and well-ordered freedom. Amidst tremendous cheering the resolution seconded by Mr. Charles Fenwick M.P., was carried unani- mously. The other business was conducted quite quietly. Mr. Acland was re-ected president, and in his address he passed so rapid review the political happenings of the year, and spoke hopefully of the immediate political future. He dwelt on the used of a plan to make the Parliamentary machine move more quickly, and he was cheered warmly for " his sugges- tion that the Government should not for a moment entertain the idea of debating all over again next year in the House of Commons the Education question. Difficult as is the situation before the Government qr. Acland saes no cause for despondency. and he has implicit faith that the Prime Minister's firmness, sagaciv and sympathy for popular causes will bring to his aid all the support he may need to advance his oroiPcted legislation for social reform. Mr. Rlbert Bird, wh ) wta r:)-elected hen. treasurer, • WAS able to tell the delagates that the attempt to raise the income of the Federation by stelseription has suc- ceeded beyond expectation. The present annual sub- sot iption list amounts to R,3,05-1, which is the highest total the Federation ha ri ever received. In the evening the delegates attended at the Gaildhall a reception given by Mr. C. H. R rdford and the Recep- tion Committee of the Plpmouth Liberal Association.
Notes From Mr. G. E. Parker. THE AMIOCT'ANCE OF TRE S.D.F. We have received the following from Mr. C. E. Parker (President of the Warrington Liberal Aesociation.)
June sth

g)od time on Wednesday Getting to Plymouth in evening, and casting about for some place to spend the evening I hesitated between a theatre and a meet- ing under the auspices of the Social Democratic Federation which had been timed to anticipate the Liberal meetings and was specially called to unmask the Liberal Party. Being some‘vhat fond of a row I selected the Socialist gathering and going bravely passed the theatre doors I found a place as near the platform as possible. Itrs. Bridges Adams was delivering an earnest and eloquent address, the key- note of which was the value of child life and the nation's responsibility in relation t ) its safeguarding. At the close of the address the lady received well merited anplaus4, to which I was glad to contribute. Arr. Harry Qeelch, who was advertised as the editor of " Justice " followed. ID appeared to think it necessary to apologize to the meeting that Nlrs. A.dams had not "gone for" the Laheral Government and proceeded to make 110 for her deficieneiei in this respect. He pro- ceded io tell us how the electors had expected great "things of the Liberals, how the members of the S-.D.F. liad-expected nothing and inasmuch as the Govern-

meat had done nothing :—that is for the people—the Liberal electors were disappointed while the members of the S.D.F. could now say "I told you so." This was somewhat unfair to a Government that in its first session had passed more measures directly benefiting the workers than any Government of which we have any records, and many in the audience felt it to be so. At the close of the address I was pleased to hear a voice which seemed familiar, putting s pertinent question. The questioner was 6.tr. Thomas Barnes, of Warrington, who instancing a few of the measures passed last session, asked how could it be truthfully said that the Government had done nothing. The answer appeared to me to be somewhat of a shuffle, and indicated that the speaker did not quite mean what his audience distinctly understood he said. I question if exaggeration and over statement ,ever permanently advance any cause, and the belittling of the motives and efforts of those in all parties other than one's own, is not a very worthy or wise method of political warfare. There are good earnest men in all parties, and the attempt of the Socialist or any other party to monopolize all the virtues, and to attribute to their opponents all the vices of our human nature, conflicts with the sense of fair play and justice with which, happily, all men are fairly liberally endowed.

There was one point in the address of Mr. Quelch which called for protest. There was the assumption all through that the Socialist party had a right to speak in the name of the whole of the working classes, indeed in the name of all who work, and on the other hand that the Liberal party represented property interest, and that only. Inasmuch as the legislation, passed last session, and in progress this session,is as a whole in the direction of curtailing property rights in directions where they invade human rights it seems not a little absurd to imply that the Liberal party is a capitalist one and that the Socialist party has the sole right to represent the workers and speak in their name. That they represent an earnest and fairly large proportion of the workers no one will deny, but they are only a section, and they appear to require to be often reminded of the fact.
AT THE FEDERATION MEETINGS,
June GM

We are now at the Federation meetings. I find Warrington strongly represented in the persons of Messrs. John Willett, Thomas Barnes, Joseph Elwell, J. Morton, J. Howes, jun., and, I think, J. T. Locker. The Federation meeting has just decided by a majority vote to alter a rule so as to make it impossible for a woman to become a member of the Executive. There are present about 150 women delegates.lt seems a very illogical position to take up to allow women to attend as delegates invested with full powers from their Associations, and then to pass a special rule to debar them from one of the rights of membership. To be consistent the Federation should have decided either to admit women and give them all the rights of membership or to affirm that it is a men's Federation and only men are to have any part in it. There is still a good deal of prejudice and a good deal of inconsistency even in Liberal Federations. The speech we have just listened to of the Right Hon. Thomas Shaw, Lord Advocate of Scotland, has been without doubt the speech of the morning. I had never before seen or heard Mr. Shaw, and his power and force came as a surprise to many besides mypelf. His general appearance, his dress, the case in which his brains are stored, gave no outward promise of any- thing beyond the Ordinary. When he began to speak the want of flow in his speech, the absence of rhetoric, the awkwardness of his gesturss, appeared sufficient to prevent any speech from becoming a success. But we were so mto be made to realise that these things, important in their place, could be made to become altogether subordinate if the speaker has a message to deliver, a message that he feels with his whole heart. There is no question about the genuineness of the Liberal princirles of Scotland's Lord Advocate. He sees that the House of Lords is the chief impediment to the embodiment of these principles in the laws of the country. Speaking with all the authority of a Cabinet Minister and from personal conviction he declared that the time had come when elected repre- sentatives of the people should be master of the destinies of those who chose them: He declared— a declaration punctuated by cheers approving its truth— that " the House of Lords had never supported an unpopular cause that was right, and never resisted a popular demand that was wrong." No better stimulus than Mr. Shaw's speech could have been given to representatives of Libera,lism.With such a sample of" C.B.'s "Cabinet the party can rest assured that there will be no turning back on the part of our leaders in this matter and that this fight will be fought to a finish and that such leaders are worthy of the most strenuous backing that the party can give them. C.E.P.

div.head: SIR JO HN KIRK.
div.p: SIR JO HN KIRK.
Congratulations From Warrington.

Last week Mr. J. Marsh, secretary of the Warrington Ragged School and Mission, wrote to Sir John Kirk, congratulatin,, him upon the honour he recently received at the hands of the King. Mr. Marsh wrote: "I desire to convey to you on behalf of the Warrington Ragged School and Mission our hearty congratulations at the distinguished honour which it has pleased his Majesty the King to confer upon you in recognition of your work amongst the poor children of London. We earnestly pray Almighty God will spare your life for many years to come to enjoy so marked an appreci- ation from our Sovereign's hand, and that your efforts to train the children under your care to become God- fearing citizens will be the means of stimulating others to t eke an interest in this most useful and really philanthropic work. In Warrington the news of your elvevation has been received with considerable satilfaction, especially by those who had the pleasure of listening to your Anniversary Sermons." Last week end Sir John Kirk replied as follows:—"! beg you will convey to your Committee my hearty appreciation and thanks for the kind resolution of con- gratulation. I recognize that his Majesty in bestowing the unexpected honour, meant thereby to showapprecia- tion to all workers in the community who are striving to help their fellows, young and old, to a better citizen- ship and a higher life."

div.head: HALE'S TOURS OF THE WORLD.
div.p: HALE'S TOURS OF THE WORLD.
White City, Manchester.

Hales Tours of the world is the only genuine, legiti- mate, and possible enterprise and entertainment of its scope and kind—nothing approaching misrepresentatiox or deception is ever, or for one moment, tolerated ; and where the conclusive proof of perfect and spotless realism, educational value and recreation is unanimously overwhelming, as voiced in unqualified admiration.and recommendation, spread broadcast upon the pages of the Press everywhere. It is the grandest and most cosmopolitan object teacher ever projected by the exceptional experience and executive genius of man, scrupulously truthful in Avery respect with every feature announced,every reference authentic, and every endorse- ment and criticism correct in spirit. It is something which intelligence and morality approve, because it is not trashy, but the perpetuation and reproduction of all the principal countries of the world. It is an exceptional and remarkable fact, repeatedly demonstrated by experi- ence under exacting circumstances, that when people find out what Halo's Tours of the World really is, they not only patronise it, but return to it again and again, and each recurring visit finds fresh food for reflection, wonder and delight, and all the more appreciate its extraordinary magnitude, 3, n d its exclusive merit and magnetism. The record of its reception wherever exhibited, may be cited in its behalf as a test of both its popularity and educational merits, not only *ithout precedent or parallel, but entirely beyond the reach of any other kind of exhibition, and which will stand for ever unrivalled. Viewed dispAssionately Hate's Tours of the World is not a mere amusement, but a tremen- dous force and a power in educating the people, as well as a picturesque illustrator of travel, which is conceded to be " the 13,,ist educator of mankind."

The Council fully under- stood that the Water Committee as a Committee had no jurisdiction over the contract but that the Joint Committee was to have full control and act with the Town Clerk in any matters concerning the contract. div.head: APPOINTMENT OF AN ARBITRATOR.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF AN ARBITRATOR.

The famous Lawson contract gave rise to another long and heated debate at the meeting of the Warring- ton Town Council on Tuesday evening. In the absence of the Mayor, the chair was occupied by Alderman Pierpoint. Both the Mayor and the Town Clerk were away in London on public business. At a meeting of the Water Committee a report was received from the Town Clerk upon "the position of the action of Lawson v. the Corporation, that he had taken out a summons to dismiss the action on the ground that the plaintiff was bound to go to arbitration under the agreement, and that the plaintiff was prepared to refer the matters in dispute to an arbitrator, but objected to the appointment of Mr. James Deas." "The Town Clerk stated that unless the Com- mittee had an objection to Mr. George Hill, of Man- chester, he proposed to agree to the appointment of him as arbitrator. It was resolved That the matter be left in the hands of the Town Clerk." ' Alderman EVANS moved and Councillor DUNCAN seconded the adoption of the minutes. The CHAIRMAN said he occupied a rather novel position as he came prepared to ask the Chairman a question and found himself acting as Chairman. He was concerned with the minute with regard to the appoint- ment of an arbitrator. He wanted to ask the Town Clerk what steps he had taken with reference to the minute, because it seemed to him that the Town Clerk had referred a question of very great importance to the Corporation to the Water Committee instead of—as he (the speaker) thought be ought to have done—to a committee appointed on December 4th, 1906 to inquire into all matters affecting Lawson's contract, with power to deal witn Lawson's claim in its entirety. The com- mittee consisted of ten members of the Council in addition to the ten members of the Water Committee, making a committee of twenty, which was surely big ienough to deal with any matter affecting the interests of Warrington with respect to the Lawson contract. It was a very singular fact that the committee was boycotted—or should he say ignored ?—from the very commencement by all the members of the Water Committee.
Councillor STOTT : I object to that. Alderman FoasirAw : So do I.
Councillor STOTT : I am a member of the Water Committee and have attended meetings of the spec ial committee.

Alderman PrERPOINT said he was sorry he made that statement and would withdraw it. He certainly was under the impression that the members of the Water Committee deliberately ignored the formation of the Special Committee. He could not understand how it was that the rown Clerk should not submit this particular matter to the properly elected committee and go instead to the Water Committee uho had taken no part in the investigation the Special Committee had carried on. It must be within the knowledge of the Council that the Investigation Committee which was appointed prior to the Joint Com- mittee went to a very great deal of work, and that Committee was empowered by the Council to call in whatever expert evidence it required. They called in Mr. Girside, an eminent civil engineer, well versed in all matters appertaining to the sinking of wells and coal mines. They received his report which was most voluminous and instructivc and he(Alderman Pierpoint) believed the information contained in it would be beneficial to any arbitrator who was investi- gating the case. Where were they ? Alderman Bolton was appointed chairman of the joint committee. Some- one said the other night that he (Alderman Pierpoint) was chairman and that he had not asserted himself as he ought to have done and seen that the committee was not over-ridden. Councillor STOTT : Alderman Bolton was chairman of the original committee but Alderman Pierpoint was appointed chairman of the joint committee. The CHAIRMAN : Is that so ? VOICES: Yes.

The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: I suggest that if the Council wants to discuss the merits of the case, it should adjourn into committee. The CHAIRMAN: I won't say anything that will have its effect on any trial. All I want to settle is this : did the Council empower the committee to carry out everything connected with the action? I say it did. What right has the Town Clerk,what right has the Water Committee to take upon itself to over-ride the proper duties of the Joint Committee? (Hear, hear.) Are we children in arms ? Are we not competent to carry out this kind of work, or is it for some other reason that I won't mention? What I want to know is whether this Council to-night is going to affirm that we are the proper committee to deal with it or whether the matter is to lie just as it is, in the hands of the Town Clerk, empowered by the Water Committee? Therefore I move an amendment: That the minute referring to the appointment of Mr. George Hill as arbitrator in the action Lawson v. Warrington Corporation be not confirmed, and that it be referred to the sub-committee appointed to serve— - The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: You can't do that.
The CHAIRMIN : I wanted you to send it back and refer it to the joint committee. Alderman TiNmoN : You are out of order, Mr. Chairman.

The CHAIRMAN: I know it. (Laughter.) Alderman EVAKS said that at the Town Council meet- ing in April the Town Clerk reported that he had been served with a writ for £36,425, at the suit of Mr. George Lawson, being the balance claimed on his account for work done and materials supplied, and it was resolved on the reconaraendation of the Water Com- mittee that the Town Clerk be instructed to defend the action.
The CHAIRMAN moved that the minute with regard to Mr. Hill's appointment be referred back._ _.
Councillor: ^CRAWLER seconded. He believed there was a resolution of the Council that Mr. Hill should not he appointed. . .

The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: No. A resolution was brought forward but withdrawn. Councillor WILDING : It was referred back. The DEPUTY TowN CLERK (having consulted the minutes) : It was withdrawn, as I said before. Alderman TINNION said he was somewhat surprised at the action the Chairman had taken, after the intimation, tie was almost going to say promise, Alderman Pierpoint gave at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee, that as it was inadvisable to raise the matter he would not take any action at present and he hoped other members would not, as it would be prejudicial to the interests of the Corporation. It was very difficult to discuss the matter in open Council without by some slip of the tongue saying something that might prejudice this very important matter. In his opinion a very satisfactory answer had been given by the Town Clerk, and he could not for the life of him see why the matter had again been raised in public. Probably there might be a time when public discussion of the action of the Water Committee and the Town Clerk and the possible ignoring of the Joint Committee could take place and the blame be put on the proper shoulders. He (Alderman Tinnion) Pointed out at the General Pur- poses Committee, and -the Town Clerk certainly proved it, that by public discussion they had done considerably more harm than good. They had al!eady damned one arbitrator in the eyes of the Court, and they were going the best way about it to damn another. He advised the Council to be very careful not to pass the amendment. He was surprised that the chairman should propose such an amendment, knowing the grave issues that were at stake, particularly after the exhaustive discussion they had the other night, and after the full, if not satisfactory explanation of the Town Clerk as to his conduct. The Town Clerk was present at the coin- mittee meeting to defend his action. He was respon- sible for the proper legal steps being taken. He (Alderman Tinnion) hoped the Council would discuss the matter in such a way that nothing could be said to prejudice their interests. He suggested that the question be adjourned until the case had been settled. That was the advice he tendered to the committee and he thought it was accepted by all parties,certainly by Alderman Pierpoint,ancl he( Alderman Tinnion) congratu- lated him on having seen the wisdom of not pressing the the matter to an issue at once. There was not the slightest doubt that more harm could be done at the present time than good. If there was any good to be done, it was after they had settled the ease and not before.

Councillor LORD supported the amendment and said he was rather surprised at the remarks of the previous speaker. Alderman Tinnion would have them come to the rescue when it was too late. He (Councillor Lord) must say that he was surprised at the action of the Town Clerk in this matter. He had defied the law of the country ; he had defied the Council ; and he had defied the committee; and he (Councillor Lord) for one should resent it. The action of the Town Clerk throughout the case had been most strange. After the Council had appointed Mr Garside to investigate the matter, the Town Clerk got the Water Committee to pass a resolution to appoint Mr. George Hill as arbitrator, before Mr. Garside had gone into the matter. He (Councillor Lord) was not going to discuss the merits or demerits of the Lawson contract. What he was discussing was the action of the Town Clerk and his treatment of the Council, and he hoped the members would resent it. He wanted to know what was the Town Clerk's motive in the way he had conducted himself. What was there behind all this' They heard that Mr. George Hill was going to be appointed arbitrator long before it was introduced before the Water Committee. He could not understand it at all. He could not see the moves, and he for one would support the amendment that the action of the Town Clerk be undone, with a view to the matter going to the proper Committee. Why the Town Clerk should ignore the Committee he himself knew best. Councillor WILKINSON said he would like to know how ranch longer the Corporation of Warrington or certain members of it were going to sit under the con-
The Town Clerk Criticised—Lively Debate.

trol of one or two members of the Council— Councillor LORD: Under the control of the Town Clerk. Councillor WILKINSON (continuing) : Members who seem to fancy but who, during the time I have known them, have never shown me anything wherein I could think they had exceptional ability beyond anyone else in the Council.

The CHAIRMAN asked Councillor Wilkinson to stick to the principle under discussion and not to make it a personal matter. Councillor WiLKissoN : I am not getting personal unless you take it as meaning yourself (interruption). I may say you are amongst them. (Cries of" Chair.") Ido not say that with any disrespect. Alderman Pier- point knows me. He is a man of my kidney. He can stand a lot without feeling insulted. (Laughter.) Times without number we }lye matters of this kind introduced before the Council, that would not be intro- duced if they concerned our own private businesses. To-night words might be dropped that would be prejudical to the interests of Warrington in the case. As a big stake holder in the town and as a man who will have to bear his fair share of any loss, I would like to know how long we are going to sit under this banner. Whatever is going on, whatever a committee authorises—with men of greater ability than some mem- bers of the Council possess—we have a certain section continually coming in office and leading some deluded person astray. (Laughter.) There is something wrong here.
Councillor ASHCROFT : He is not speaking to the minutes.

Councillor WILKINSON : I shall allow the Chairman to put me in order, and not you. As a Warrington man with some interest at stake I want to know how much longer we are going to suffer under the dictates of one or two men—

The CHAIRMAN : That has nothing to do with the amendment. Do speak to the amendment. Councillor WILKINsox : I am speaking to the amendment and showing how foolish you have been to bring it forward. (Cries of " chair.") The CHAIRMAN : I appeal to the members as to whether that is in order. (Cries of "chair " and " order.") Councillor ViTH.Krssos : I withdrawn() word foolish. Some people remind me of a duck that can only say "quack." (Laughter.) Continuing he again asked how much longer they were going to be deluded by one or two men. The Town Clerk moved in the matter at a very critical period and he had not ignored the sub- committee. That sub-committee had been so much like a crawling snail since its last meeting that he gnostic ned whether the Town Clerk knew it actually existed. (Laughter.)He (the speaker)was a member of that com- mittee and the Chairman was the convener,but for months they had never had a meeting. In the meantime certain action was being taken. Who had to take action except the Town Clerk? The dilatory ways of the Chairman in not calling the committee together showed that the committee was serving no good purpose. The CHAIRMAN : I must take exception to you say- ing something that is not true. (Cries of "chair.") Councillor WILKINSON: Too long a period expired before we were called together again, if the matter was of such great importance. The CHAIRMAN: I expect my servants to do my work. I don't do my servants' work. Speak to the amendment.

Councillor WILKINSON: lam speaking to it. The CIIAIRAIAN : I don't think you are. Councilior WILKINSON : I am trying to show that you should dot have brought forward such an amend- ment. If you were wanting to ruin the town of War- rington you could not do better. What have we got for the inquiry? When my friends who have a stake in Warrington speak to me on the subject- Councillor WILDING : Is this speaking to the amendment?
Councillor WILKINSON : Will you mind your own business !
The CHAIRMAN: Really, I must rule you out of order.

Councillor WILKiNsos : I am speaking to the amendment. (Cries of "Chair.") The CHAIRMAN: Either speak to the amendment pr take your seat, or else I shall leave this chair. Councillor WILKINSON: Your amendment is that the resolution shall not pass. Well, I oppose it. Councillor NIELD submitted that the dignity of the Council would be hest consulted by putting off that acrimonious discussion till a more suitable time. There were great issues involved, and the least they said about it the better. It was not improbable that the chairman had good grounds to advance on behalf of what be had said in regard to the Town Clerk having acted without consulting him and his brother members of the com- mittee, but a discussion involving that principlb could be very well postponed. He appealed to the good sense of the Press not to report what had been said. Alderman FORSHAW thought with Councillor Nield that the least said the better. The matter was sub jtulice and if the amendment were carried, it would not have any effect simply because ha understood Mr. Hill had already been appointed by the Court. Councillor PEMBERTON said he understood that under the Municipal Corporations Act no act of a Committee was legal until it had received the consent of the Coun- cil. He therefore submitted that now was the proper time to refer the matter back. It was a wonderful thing how members of the Council seemed to forget, not wilfully, that they were representing the ratepayers outside the Council. They were not representing any clique or the Corporation servants, but the outside public looked to every member to conduct the business of the town in the identical way that he would conduct his own private business. He asked the Council to give him their attention without prejudice, and to look at the matter fairly and squarely as business men. They let the contrut for £24,400. Let them follow that con- tract, as far as the Corporation was concerned. The CHAIRMAN : I would not discuss the contract.

Councillor PEmßunTos: : lam not going to discuss anything with regard to the case now before the Court. I am only going to discuss matters that have come out here in public. I only wish it were possible to tell the Council and the public exactly what the result of the inquiry has been. Unfortunately because this action is pending we have been unable to make the result of our inquiry public. I won't touch on anything to prejudice the Corporation in any way. My whole object in the position I have taken up has been to save the rate- payers of Warrington enormous expenditure. For three years the Lawson contract went on. I venture to say there were not two gentlemen in the Council who knew how it was going on. The CHAIRMAN : I dont think any good will be obtained by that course of discussion. What we want to discuss is the principle—whether the committee has been treated rightly or wrongly. Don't let us go into figures or have any discussion as to how the contract has been carried on. It was far from my intention to elicit anything of the kind. I do not question the ability of Mr. Hill. What I say ?Is that the rown Clerk has taken upon himself a course of action which I think be ought not to have taken and I want the Council to affirm it or otherwise.

Councillor PEMBERTON said the matter was the most important that was ever before the Council. He wanted to show how the Town Clerk's conduct commenced in the initial stage. This was not the first instance. The CHAIRMAN : But I am only referring to this particular instance where something has been done referring to one Committee, whereas I contend that he ought to have referred it to another Committee. Councillor PEMBERTON said this was not the first time the Town Clerk had disobeyed in regard to a resolution of the Council. When he (Councillor Pemberton) raised the question of Lawson's contract and said he believed the claim would be more like £50,000 than £21,000 he was called a very ugly word by the Chairman of the Committee. Ho convinced the Council that he ought to have access to the papers and they passed a resolution that any member of the Com- mittee should have aceess to the minutes and papers relating to the contract. He went to Mr. Deas' office. Councillor WILKINSON: is this speaking to the amendment? I must ask you, considering my past treatment—
The CELIERMAN : Councillor Pemberton is trying to show that this is mot the first occasion.

Councillor WILKINSON : Has that anything to do with your amendment? (Cries of " chair.") The CHAIRMAN : You must let me conduct the meeting. I hope Councillor Pemberton will not travel too wide. I could have travelled very wide if I wanted but I avoided it. _ _ _

Councillor PEAIRF.RTON said he went to the water engineer and Mr. Dees said he had not the contracts or the bills and that they were at the Town Clerk's office. He went to the Town Clerk accompanied by a witness and said he wanted to see Lawson's contract and the bills in accordance with the resolution of the Council. The Town Clerk said : "I shall not show them to you." That was when it commenced. He ventured to say there was not another Town Clerk in England in a town of the size of Warrington who ever did that in the course of his life.

The CHAIRMAN : I don't think I would go as wide as that. Let us keep to the principle. Councillor PEMBERTON said the Investigation Com- mittee recommended that Air. Garside should be engaged to go through the contract on their behalf and measure up the work. The Council aereed to that and yet, strangely, in spite of that the Water Committee brought before the Council the appointment of Mr. George Hill. The Council sent that minute back and the committee went on with the inquiry and sat a great many times,with the result that a great deal of informa- tion was obtained. When Mr. Lawson threatened the action the Joint Committee was appointed, the terms of the appointment being as wide as possible. The comraitteee met, but only one member of the Water Committee attended the meetings. During the whole of the meetings the Deputy Town Clerk attended, the Town Clerk not being presentt once. The committee

div.head: LATE MR. THOMAS HALL. -- Memorial Gifts to Goiborne-street
div.p: THE LATE MR. THOMAS HALL. -- Memorial Gifts to Goiborne-street
Church.

The late Mr. Thomas Hall, a pillar of Nonconformity and a staunch temperance worker, was identified with Golborne-street Baptist Church from its formation, and Thursday evening witnessed the presentation to that Chnrch of some fitting memorials to this devoted and honoured worker who is held in affectionate remem- branch by a very wide circle. Mr. Hall was one of the most ardent supporters of the Independent Order of Rechabites in this town and neighbourhood, and the Council of the Warrington District decided to place on permanent record their appreciation of his work by presenting to Golborne-street church a handsome carved oak Communion table. At the same time a number of members of the church and friends took the opportunity' of paying their tribute to Mr. Hall's services at Golborne-street by giving to the church and school a platform desk and chair, an enlarged framed photograph of Mr. Hall, and a set of carved oak collecting plates. There was a large attendance at the special service on Thursday evening when the gifts were handed over to the keeping of the church officars. The various tents comprising the Warrington district of the o:der of Rechabites were well represented. The Rev. JOHN YONGE conducted the service, and in the course of his address said it was always a pleasant and profitable thing when Christian people who held different views of truth and doctrine, could come together in acts of worship and in deeds of Christian service. So long as human nature, and thought and feeling, remained as they were, there were bound to be divergencies of opinion and differences of belief. Never, in this life at any rate, could it be reasonably expected that all Christians would think exactly alike; or hold the same views of truth or follow the same modes of worship ; or see "eye to eye" upon everything. It was hopeless to seek, it was foolish even to desire uniformity of faith and practice, either in doctrine or in ritual. And yet there were matters—and they were the greatest and most essential matters of all—in which Christians could and did agree; and it was a great joy when occasions offered whereon these essential agreements drew Christians into cordial and refreshing fellowship and co-operation. It was that "Unity of the Faith" which enabled thorn to meet that ni.ht, and it was also because they could all more or loss unite in recognizing that the late Mr. Thomas Hall was en Jpright, just, and loyal Christian man, that, although his vie-.vs on even important points were not in agreement with other views held by some of them, they could cordially meet to do honour to his memory, and take part in a ruu.ticu which would help to perpetuate that memory in years to come. Any memorial, it seemed to hirn,that helped to keep fresh and green the memory of the good and the Christian, had a helpful influence upon every susceptible mind, and for that reason he rejoiced that that Christian Church was now to have, within its con- tinual view, a tangible and handsome memorial of the late Mr. Thomas Hall. His personal acquaintance with their departed friend was but comparatively slight. He knew him, of course, as intimately associated with that church; as a strict and loyal and devout Baptist ; as an upright and honourable man ; as one held in true resrect by all who knew him best. He had been told that the Baptist Church which now for over thirty years had worshipped in that building had reason to regard Mr. Hall with affec- tionate veneration and honour, as almost if not quite absolutely its founder. The history of Lancashire Nonconformity, published a few years ago by the Rev. B. Nightingale, of Preston detailed the somewhat chequered history of that building, and it described also the changeful experiences through which the Bapiist cause in Warrington passed in its long byegone years. It described further how in 1869, on the initiative of Mr. Hall, a Baptist Church was formed, comprising some Baptist people who had formerly worshipped some- where in Buttermarket-street. A small iron chapel was erected in Rylands-street opposite what was then known as the Public Hall,and the community there worshipping became associated with Myrtle-street Church in Liver- pool. A few years passed on, when about 1876 the Golborne-street building came into the possession of the friends who worshipped in Rylands-street, and it was re-opened as a Baptist Church under the pastoral oversight of the Rev. 1. Harrison, who was pastor there when he (Mr. Yonge) was recognized as pastor at Wycliffe in November of the year just named. Mr. Hall was then the leading officer in that Church and continued to be so, with characteristic assiduity and zeal for a long number of years. There could be no doubt in the minds of any who knew him and who were witnesses of his loyal attachment and devotion to that Christian brotherhood, that the memory of Mr. Hall truly merited the handsome memorial which was being publicly presented. It would serve to keep his name a living and influential power in that camtnunity. The young people would be reminded of a man who hold the interests of that Church supreme in his esteem. Mr. Yonge related how the circular issued by the Church proposing that a Communion table should be placed in that building as a memorial, came into the hands of the District Council of the Independent Order of Rechabities who instead of merely votinga sum towards the object, most generously pledged themselves to provide the Communion table. The memorial there- fore became more than a tribute to Mr. Hall's memory as a sincere and devoted member of the Baptist Church. It was also a memorial to him as a member of a very large and distinguished and historic Order of total abitainers. For the long period of sixty years he was a member of the Order of Rechabites, and this presentation came from the Warrington district. every one of the 19 tents having contributed to it. These articles of Church furniture would testify not only to Mr. Hall's character as a Christian and a Baptist and a Nonconformist, but to his loyal adhesion to the principle and practice of total abstinence; and to his cordial support of an Order which had done so much to train the iising race, to help men and women to avoid the temptations and sorrows of drink, and to make pro- vision for the emergencies and necessities of existence. The memorial was a tribute of respect and esteem for one whom they held in memory as a true Christian and a worthy Rechabite—a man whose memory and influence should live for long years to come, as an inspiration and example for "generations yet unborn." Bro. HILL, District Chief Ruler' presided over the formal presentation, and said Bro. Hall was a thorough gentleman, and one could not help but admire his noble character.

Bro. SHAW, senior trustee, then presented the Communion table, and referred to his own connection with the Order extending over fifty yelrs. Bro. Hall was one upon whose judgment they could always rely, and they were voicing the sentiments of over 1,000 mem- bers in the Warrington district in honouring his memory.

_ Mr. FERNLEY, secretary of the presentation committee, on behalf of the subscribers, then presented the other gifts which he said were an evidence of their sincere respect for one to whom the present generation little knew the extent of its indebtedness. The desk and chair were for use in the schoolroom, a part of church life which was perhaps most dear to their departed friend's heart, for he had ever a most tender regard for the children. The photograph was taken twenty years ago and depicted Mr. Hall at the time of his retirement from their midst. Mr. Fernley then gave a brief sketch of Mr. Hall's Christian work, commencing with his attachment to the old Dallam-lane chapel. Humility
and conscientiousness were outstanding features of hifi. character.

Mr. B. FEW, president of the church, accepted the gifts. Mr. Hall, he said, was a convinced and pro' nounced B,lptist and served that church in every con- ceivable capacity. He was very dogmatic, wa s moves by a high sense of duty, and was a tender and tactf sympathiser.
The presentation articles in oak were supplied 11 Messrs. J. 4. Greenhalgh and Co.
